water and power.

Asiatic fleet nearly sank member of

ary history.

mantle, was born Joseph Djugashvili.

steel

president of the Council of Peoples
Commissars, Is better known as Molo-
toff, OF hammer"


Leon Trotsky exiled from the Soviet
State, was born Leon Bronstein.


Returned to Real Name.


So far as is known, Michael Frunze,
late successor to Trotsky as commisSar
for war, was the only prominent Com
munist here who ever returned to his
real name from revolutionary alias.


Some of the other better-known per-
sonages here who still retain their as
sumed names are Maxim Gorky, whose
real name is Peshkov and whose alias
means bitter; Karl Radek, formerly
Sobolson, and Gregory zinovieff and
Leo Kameneff, who have since followed
Trotsky into political oblivion. They
originally were named Rosenfeld and

Many garden makers who have
depended upon gladioli for cut
flowers in past years are turn
ing to dahlias because of the
new pest called thrips, which is
making trouble for gladiolus
growers. If the smaller flowered
dahlias are chosen, they will
make excellent cut blooms. Any
soil that will grow corn will grow
good dahlias. but drainage Is Of
great Importance. Dahlia plants
will not flourish where the
ground is wet or heavy. Clay
soil, however, can be hghtened
by using loose, coarse manure or
leaf mold. Sometimes the soil is
too sandy, but that condition can
be overcome by adding well-rot-
ted manure. Most dahlias make
large growth, and for that reason
should stand 18 inches apart,
with twice that distance between
the rows. Six inches Is about
the right depth for planting the
average dahlia root.

TINE finest iron player in the
world of golf probably has
L fewer aces to his credit
than any man who has
been knocking the ball toward dis
tant pins over the same period of
time.


Tommy Armour, one-time holder of
all the major professional champion
ships of the world, universally rated
the finest iron player in the world
today, has made only two holes in one
during his lengthy career on the links.
Tommy has been playing golf for 80
years, off and on, for during the
years he served IN the British Army
during the war there were more i'm
portant matters on his mind than bag
ging brides. During those 30 years
Tommy has been consistently as close
to the pin with his iron shots as any
man who has played the game of golf,
and yet only twice has he been able to
bag the elusive ace. Players of in
finitely inferior skill have bagged far
more holes in one than the Black Scot.
but Tommy himself-the master iron
player Of his generation--has had the
supreme thrill only twice.

BY the Associated Press


Inc cold wave from the Far North
country today continued to hold much
OF the North American continent in its
grip, bringing with 1t slowly mounting
death list, while the storm-tossed
North Atlantic imperilled shipping.


The weather man, meanwhile held
out little hope for relief today from
the fr1gid blast which affected the en-
tire country east of the Rocky Noun
tainS, after recording new lows for this
tlme OF the year in various parts of the
Midwest, including below at Bemidji
MINI. Parts of the East also were
hard hit.


pennsylvania counted a total of six
dead during the past two days, with a
new storm sweeping the northwestern
section OF the State, already buried
under a heavy snowfall. Two hunters
died in Ohio from over-exertion, and
the frigid blasts brought suffering to
Island inhabitants in Lake Erie, caught
short of fuel


One death from exposure was reported
in st. Paul. Detroit shivered with 8
above zero, and thousands of homeless
sought shelter in Chicago, which broke
50-year record for November Is, with
10 above zero yesterday.


Fears that the death list would he
increased by the loss of two coast
guards men in picket boat on Lake
Superior were dissippated when they
were reported safe on Madeline Island


Mild weather prevailed on the Pacific
Coast.


While Western Ontario dug itself out
OF the worst snowstorm in two decades,
sailors on the Great Lakes today cast
anxious eyes to the bays and channels
and hoped the thin coating of ice would
become no thicker.


The list of wrecks and near wrecks
remained unchanged today In the past
week. one vessel, the tug Florence, has
sunk. Another, the D. z. Calender. is
still aground near Long Point in Lake
Erie. Several others which were strand
ed have been pulled off, and the United
States Coast Guard boat 1908, missing
since Sunday with O two-man crew,
has finally reached port after being re-
ported lost.


Low water has congested the lower
st. Lawrence canals, and marine off,
cials fear the lack of constant move
ment may permit them to freeze up.
Even today, Ice was forming in the
small lakes below Sault Ste. Marie, and
threatening to block vessels from
reaching that port from the lower
lakes. The "bottle-neck" of Hay and
Mud Lakes some years ago trapped q
number of vessels In the ice, and they
remained there for weeks.


The land storm had assumed grave
proportions today. In the Western
Ontario areas, particularly, heavy
snow has fallen and railway snow
plows were being prepared for the ffrst
time in nine years.

JONESBORO, Ill, August 11.-Nve
young Duquoin miners were found
guilty by Circuit Court jury here last
night of the murder Of Laverne Miller,
14-year-old school girl.


Four of the defendants-Robert
Shingleton, Sam Ferro, Otis Battagla
and Barney Bosetto-were sentenced to
life imprisonment. Emery Albers was
given a 40-year sentence.


None of the five showed any emotion
when the verdict was read.


Attorneys for the State had asked
the death penalty.


The Miller girl, a daughter Of a
Duquoin United Mine worker, was
fatally wounded by shots fired from
speeding car as she sat in her home
studying her high school lessons the
night of April 6.


The convicted men were affiliated
with the Progressive Miners organiza-
tion. Counsel for both the State and
the defense, in final arguments. at
tributed the murder indirectly to the
bitterness between the Progressive and
the United Mine Workers in southern
Illinois.

rains.


Thousands were rendered homeless.

isolated or under water tonight.

quarter were leveled by the almost I'M
precedented floods. Residents fed to
higher ground.

zens, was straining its levees and some

threatened.

was isolated following the washing out
of bridge. Families living there were
brought out by boat in scores of thrill
ing rescues. Eight persons were re-
ported in bad condition from exposure.

with trees and wreckage. The rain
which began at pm. yesterday con-
tinued through the afternoon.


Gov. Cardenas and Mayor Gales
called out all city and state facilities
for rescue and relief Of affected inhab-
itants.

President Roosevelt, aided by his
family, played Santa Claus to White

stretched hands of children, of police

Four very dirty little penguins
arrived at the zoo yesterday after
noon after six days trip across
the continent.


Ten minutes after the birds had
been put in the big flight cage in
the Bird House four immaculate
little penguins emerged from the
pool and began giving their feath-
ers an additional grooming.


The penguins fairly beamed with
delight over their bath. The most
amiable of little creatures, they
have not the slightest fear Of
man. They permitted DR.. William
Mann, superintendent of the ZOO,
to play with them and ate their
first Washington supper from
keepers hand.


According to DR.. Mann all the
birds of the Galapagos Islands,
from which the zoos new pen
gums came, are entirely tame.
They seldom see human being
and those they see are always
friendly.


The penguins were a gift of the
San Diego, Cal, Geological Gar
dens to Washington. With them
arrived a pair of flightless cor
morants and an assorted collec-
tion of boobies. The latter, birds
not men, have never before been
exhibited in an Eastern ZOO.


The name, BOBBY, was given
them long ago by British sailors
who visited their island breeding
place. Finding the birds tame the
sailors decided they were stupid
and labeled them for all time
with most unfair cognomen.
They are a species of gannet.

BY the Associated Press.


MADRID, December 11-A general
strike, supported by Syndicalists, spread
over Spain today as violence subsided
following the capture of the Villaneuva
military barracks, in which rebel forces
had withstood a terrific bombardmenr.


Despite the increase of strikes, COM
merce and industry generally went or
as usual, apparently confident the walk
out movement would collapse. Only
in a few places did Socialists CO.
operate with the Communists and An
archists who fomented the bloody dis
orders Of the past three days.


Government troops, supported by
cannon, early today charged the VIII
laneuva barracks, where the rebel flag
had flown since yesterday, and took
slain.


These known dead brought to IS the
number slaiD in the anarchist revolu-
tionary movement which broke out Fri
day and which flared with new vio-
lence in Central and Northeastern
Spain yesterday.


Attack at Dawn.


Throughout the night the civilian
defenders. under a renegade army ser
geant, withstood machine gun fire.
Finally two army planes were ordered
from Madrid to bomb the barracks.
But when dawn came and the planes
had not arrived, the colonel in charge
of the troops ordered the final charge.


1t was not known whether the SER
geant leader of the uprising was among
the dead, as the bidies were all dressed
in civilian clothes and unidentified.


Assault troops and civil guards were
dispatched to surrounding towns TO
overcome Extremist manifestations.


Meanwhile, with the situation in
other parts of the revolt affected region
remaining tense, the government con-
sidered declaring martial law.


An attempt to burn the fourteenth
century Church of San Marina, which
recently was declared a national monu-
ment, was frustrated by police, but they
did not succeed in extinguishing the fire
until after valuable hand-carved doors
had been destroyed.


Madrid was fairly quiet today.


Bomb Factory Discovered.


Police discovered bomb factory in
Madrid, in which they said incendiary
bombs of a type used in the Barcelona
terrorist campaign we're being manufac-
tured. The bombs we're found to have
attached vessels containing mixture
of gasoline and benzine. Two of those
arrested said they were designed for use
in firing converts.


At Seville, railroad workers joined
the strike movement, paralyzing traffic
Sixteen machinists and flremen were
arrested and number of factories
closed.


Extremists attempted to burn Ma
drid orphanage housing more than 1000
children. but the fire was extinguished
with little damage.


Firemen found the doors had been
saturated with gasoline before they
were ignited. The government ordered
the arrest of Syndicalist workers on the
railroads when the Syndicalist Railway
Union decided to join the strike.


Early this morning Barcelona au-
thorities stationed IA trucks carrying
machine gunners in districts held by
Extremists to halt the terrorist bomb
ings and incendiarism.


Barcelona suffered from sporadic OUT
breaks of fighting Sunday, along with
Madrid, and numerous towns through
out Central and Eastern Spain were
subjected to literal reign Of terror.

BY the Associated Press


GRAND RAPIDS, Mich, December
23.--Beaten, criminally attacked and
shot three times through the head. the
body of Miss Margaret Peevey. a 22-
year-old deaf mute, was found TODAY in
a meadow 2 miles beyond the city
limits.


Identification was made first at the
morgue here by Patrolman Thomas
Marshall, a friend of the family, and
later confirmed by the young woman's
father, Edward G. Peevey. Her mother
died eight years ago.


The body was discovered shortly after
noon today by Frank Zuidema, farmer.
Apparently it had been lying in the
neld for "a hours or more The cloth
ing was torn; two teeth had been
knocked out, one bullet fired through
the forehead and one through each
cheek


Missing Since Thursday,


Coroner Simeon LIE Roy, who said
the girl had been criminally attacked.
explained that because the body was
frozen his autopsy would have to be
postponed temporarily.


Peevey said his daughter had been
missing since Thursday, but that be-
cause she had disappeared once before.
about year ago, he had not been espe-
cislly worried.


He said the girl had been deaf since
she was 3 years old and had never
learned to talk He said she had
number OF deaf mute friends with whom
she went out occasionally, but that he
had no reason to believe any of them
had been with her since she left home.


Although admitting they were with
out clue to the girls companion prior
to the attack, officers advanced the
theory she might have been accosted
by some one unaware of her inability to
talk, who, becoming angered at her 81
lerce, struck her and rendered her un-
conscious.


Beaten Before Attack.


DR.. LIE Roy said he believed the girl
might have been attacked after having
been struck.


The identification of the victim as &
deaf mute explained the presence, Off
GERS said, of a button found on her
clothing bearing the words American
Association for the Promotion of Teach
ing Speech to the Deaf" 1t also ended
a search for Miss Ora Swartwood a
teacher of the hard-of- of-hearing classes
in the Flint. Mich, public schools.


Miss Swartwood was en- route from.
Flint to her home north of Grand Rap
ids for the Christmas holidays.

FREDERICKSBURG Va, February
3.-Stafford County officers and local
police are making an intensive search
today for two white men who abducted
Caroline Musante, 13year-old daugh-
ter of Mr. and Mrs. Leo Musante, and
left her tied in the woods, where she
was found at $50 o'clock last night
suffering from cold and hunger. The
girl had not been harmed in any way
and is not expected to suffer any III
effects from her experience.


The Musante home is miles from
Fredericksburg. close to the Washington
Highway. Caroline left home yester-
day morning to take the bus for Stat
ford High School. but upon reaching the
highway she heard mans voice call
ing from the bushes. Starting to run.
the girl was warned she would be shot.
She halted and was taken into the
woods by two men using the names Of
Bill" and Harry about Is and 80
yeats old. respectively. neither of whom
was known to Caroline.


The girl was taken deep into the
woods and tied to tree while her alb
ductors questioned her about sum Of
money recently received by H. P. Por-
ter, relative and neighbor of the Mu-
santes, as damages for the death of
his 6-year- -old daughter, who was killed
by an automobile several months ago.
A threatening note in this connection
had been left in the yard of the Porter
home Saturday night.


Bill and Harry" left the girl tied
to a tree about 10 o'clock. returning
about dusk for further questioning. but
failed to elicit any information and
again departed.


When Caroline failed to return home
from school in the afternoon her FAM
lily started search and her cries were
heard about $50 o'clock last night.
Cold, hungry and highly nervous, with
her wrists swollen from the tightly
knotted rope, Caroline related her story
to officers. who Immediately started
securing the countryside for the pair
of abductors. Up to noon today they
had found no trace Of the men.

Falling overheard from fishing boat

NEW YORK, December Retail
trade, which has been the bright spot
In the general business picture in re-
cent weeks. was somewhat slower this
week.


Perhaps this was q result Of the
Thanksgiving holiday or some slacken-
ing of commercial and industrial oper-
atoms. At any rate it Is notable that
in nearly every center where retail trade
gained during the week, the result was
directly attributed to the pushing Of
the Civil Works Administration in that
locality.


National chain stores with head +.
quarters here reported satisfaction with
November trade, which generally showed
substantial increases over the same
month year ago. In every instance.
however, the chains declared that the
best gains this month came in the first
half


Retail and wholesale food prices
during the week were lower. This was
noticed in holiday goods, such Is meats
and poultry, and some Of the special
ties. though average fruits and vege-
tables, thanks to the seasonal weather
in most sections were somewhat higher
than in the preceding week or the same
holiday week year ago.


Holiday Orders Heavy.


There was a good volume of (whole-
sale) business booked in Thanksgiving
and holiday dried fruit lines. such as
raisins. imported and domestic figs,
dates, citron and other peels," Dun q
BradStreet. Inc, report in their ma
tional weekly survey of business. Dried
apricots have moved out Of the hands
Of grocers entirely and heavy exports
to Europe In recent weeks have brought
about decided f1rming up in prices
with some advances recorded in the top
grades. Peaches and pears, however,
have eased somewhat from their recent
positions Owing to the unfavorable
exchange situation, with the resultant
higher prices. importers have been ex-
tremelv cautious in their purchases
abroad, and a scarcity of some goods
exists.


Holiday items are active in the
canned goods division. but most prices
are somewhat lower than they were q
few weeks ago, although no further re-
cessions are anticipated. On the new
pack of grapefruit. prices are we'll main
tanned. Prices of imported goods, such
as crabmeat and tuna fish. have moved
higher with the decline Of the dollar.
Stocks of vegetables in the hands of
distributors are relatively light and I'M
sold goods are considerably below those
of a year ago. Unsatisfactory condi-
tions still prevail In the wholesale fish
trade, but a larger demand is expected
from hotels. clubs and restaurants fol-
lowing repeal"


Speaking Of repeal, orders continue to
pile in to glass manufacturers, espe-
cially for liquor glasses. Demand for
ordinary water goblets also has in
creased. Locally, many stores refuse to
make any promises of nearby deliveries
if the article sought is not then in stock.
Some mems furnishing departments
complain that they are being passed up
in holiday shopping this year for re.
peal wares.


Apparel Trends Mixed.


Wearing apparel this week displayed
about as mixed trends as one could
imagine. Coats barely moved Dinner
and evening gowns and sweaters were
snapped up. Fur garments moved well.
Cruise clothing and mems evening
usual Thanksgiving supplies, linens, sill
verware, glassware and kitchen utensils

slackened and Oriental rugs turned slug
gish.


Wholesale buying generally has been
reduced. Some flll-in gift orders are

been delayed. Aside from the West and
South. dry goods markets assert that
shipments are going out much quicker
than new orders are received. Mems
wooden wear is selling better than wom-
ems items

changed. Electric output recorded its
thirtieth weekly successive gain. Car
loadings for the twenty-ninth successive
time improved over those of year ago.
Lumber and bituminous coal were better
than either last week or a year ago,
the former reaching its highest orders
since october, 1880.

Freshwater eels descend from their

deposited Is not known, but the eels
ole after once spawning and the young
return In large numbers to fresh water
when they sfe two years old. This
movement takes place annually between
October and February.

Greek jurists were not satisfied a case
for extradition had been made out in
accordance with Greek law.

The splendor of the Russian imperial

ture, and the happy home life of the
peasants under the Czarist regime were
described to members of the National
Geographic Society at the Washing
ton Auditorium last night by Princess
Cantacuzene, who was introduced by
DR.. Gilbert Grosvenor, president of the
society,".


Princess Cantacuzene, who was born
In the White House during the incum-
bency Of her grandfather, u. S. Grant,
married Prince Michael Cantacuzene
and spent% nearly 20 years in Russia,
where she was q close observer OF po-
ntical and economic conditions. She
made her home in the Crimea, where
her husbands family had q splendid
chateau and vast estates, until the
wholesale massacre Of the nobility and
intellectual classes took place.


A striking change has taken place
In the costumes Of the peasants since
said. The quaint costumes that once
tionS of the country, been discarded for
Western fashions, and many Of the
native home industries have been all
but destroyed Under the new regime.
Contrary to recent Soviet propaganda,
she declared, Russian farmers used
modern farming equipment in Czarist
days and many factories were equipped
with modern machinery.


The princess remarks were illustrated
by motion pictures and lantern slides
Pictures taken 20 years ago showed the
old splendor Of Leningrad, Moscow and
other large Russian cities.

All Cuba was tense today with

soon withdraw from the fray.

HAVANA, Aug. 4 UN.SO.-Pre-
saying a victory for passive re-
sistance" where clashes at arms
failed in the past, Cuba's general
strike reached the proportions Of
a major political crisis today.


Observers predicted the early
downfall of President Gerardo
Machado as a result.


Havana was virtually paralyzed
as laborers of all classes joined
Transportation workers in what
started as bus strike week ago
and swiftly developed into an un-
precedented mass demonstration
against the Machado regime.


Printers, stevedores, and vendors
quit their posts, joining taxi drlv-
ers, street car workers, and truck
men, virtually paralyZing Havana's
industry and transportation. The
railway union were expected to
join the walkout tomorrow.


With a nationwide strike immi-
nent, Federal troops and police
were mobilized to prevent disor-
ders.


Cabinet Confers


The Machado cabinet met In
extraordinary session at the pres
idential palace, discussing meas
ures to combat the fast-spreading
strike. Federal troops and police
were modified to prevent dis
orders.


Printers, stevedores and ven
dors quit their posts today, join
ing taxi drivers, street car work
ers and truckmen.


Reliable information indicated
railway workers would join the
strike tomorrow, along with ice
men and milkmen, threatening
complete paralysis Of Havana's
industry.


Provisions Run Out


Market houses and trsdesmen
sold out the last of their supplies
this morning, with no hope OF
obtaining new provision unless
transportation workers return to
their jobs. Most of the city's
stores closed.


The eight-year regime Of Pres
ident Gerardo Machado Y MOI
ales has been marked by revolu-
tions, bombings, shootings, assas-
sinations, and a reign of terror
unprecedented in modern times.


Machado kept himself in pow
er, however, with a well-paid and
loyal army. and institution OF
reforms" in CubaS constitution
which continually postponed the
election of a successor.


Up until the present strike,
American Ambassador Sumner
Welles had been making progress
in his arbitration attempts. Early
this week, however, it became
apparent that the crisis was far
from ended. President Roose-
welt, as revealed exclusively by
international News Service IN
Washington, served emphatic no
tice that he would conclude no
new trade agreements with Cuba
until the differences between
Machado and his foes were
settled,

TOXIC, Japan, July 27.-Manchukuo
whose attitude toward the Soviet Union
has been increasingly truculent since
the start Of the negotiations in Toxic
for the sale of the Chinese Eastern
Railway, today issued two defiances
against Moscow.


The first note, coming from Chang
chun, or Hsinking. capital of the new
state, declares Manchukuo is prepared
to resort to force" unless the railroad
employs the same number-and of equal
rank-of Manchukuo citizens, mostly
Japanese, as it does Soviet subjects.


The second announcement threatens
to resort to some drastic measures
unless the Red soldiers, whom Man.
chukuo calls bandits, stop searching
Manchukuo-registered. Japanese-owned
ships on the Amur River.


Taro Shirimoto, a Japanese, repre-
senting the Manchukuo foreign Office,
filed these protests with the Soviet con-
sui at Harbin.

When the Central High basket
ball candidates trot out Monday

ured him and found him to be

MATTEAWAN, N. Y, September g.
One inmate of the State Hospital for
the Criminally Insane was shot to
death by State trooper and two others
were overcome by tear gas when officers
forced their way into small room
where four crazed men had barricaded
themselves during an attempted escape
early today.


Ray Fisher, 26, of Buffalo, leader Of
the attempted break, was killed by
Trooper Robert Calvin. Fisher had
leveled a 20 caliber revolver at Gal
win when the latter crashed through
the door.


The trooper, his gun already drawn,
fired a bullet through the young des-
perado's heart. Two Of the remaining
three were sprawled on the floor where
they had fallen, overcome by the erior-
nous amount of tear gas fired into the
room. They were James Ellis OF
Brooklyn and Skelly Marshall of New
York City.


Attacked Guard in Ward.


The oldest of the four, Reinhardt
Volz Of New York, an inmate for II
years, was found unharmed in wash
room nearby.


The men had struck a guard down
with q chair shortly after l am. and
made a dash from the large ward
where they were kept with ga other
patients. More than so guards, State
troopers and other officers had sur
rounded the room where they were
barricaded with their one revolver.


Meanwhile, the inmates in the
ward had gone on rampage, smash
ing furniture and windows in the room
where they were held with two guards
They completely wrecked the room, but
did not molest the guards.


By DAYLIGHT all the inmates were
quieted and DR.. Raymond F. c. Kieb
superintendent of the institution, said
that order had been restored. The riot
was confined to the one ward, which
had not been regarded as having any
very dangerous patients.


Two More Guns Found.


The four who led the attempted breal
were all serving terms for minor OF.
fenses, three having been committed
for assault and one for larceny.


It was not learned Immediately how
Fisher obtained the revolver or the
keys to the ward, which were found ir
his pockets.

caliber revo1vers. These were loadet

contraband weapon used by the rioter!

NEW YORK, July 81 G.N.S).
The stock market today recovered
from the sensational crash Of the
last 3 days after another wave of
forced selling from impaired
margin accounts in the forenoon.
With support in the leaders
helping to tide the list over the
fresh rush Of liquidation, the
market rallied.

bound, just as they had precipi-
tAted the collapse. National dis
tillers set the pace, rising about
3 points. Commercial solvents
snapped back 3 points, and the
other "wet" shares recovered as
well as those on the curb. The
Tennessee repeal victory helped.


The rest of the market was
more sedate but gains in a few
Of the volatile issues ran to 4
points and" more. There was
little Of the old enthusiasm on
the rally, however, and sufficient
selling developed on the bulge to
hold the list down with conSid-
cradle irregularity here and
there.

yesterdays recovery. Sterling at
one time was up cents but sold
down later. Wheat was firm in
Winnipeg while Chicago was
closed.


The weekend business reviews
reported no slackening in the
trade revival, and this helped
sentiment somewhat.

port Just before leaving the Lind
berghs talked for a short time with

personal representative to Cuba, who
took regular passenger plane for Cuba
around am.

colonel lifted the big ship from the
water and skinned over Biscayne Bay

at fairly high speed

crowd gathered at the airport as the
Lindberghs entered their p&ne. Some
of those present had been there since
dawn to get glimpse of the noted
flying pair

rated the colonel and his wife from
their small son.

Amelia Earhart Putnam, who has
flown the Atlantic twice, once by her
self, and who has flown across the
United States many times, had one of
the most exciting moments Of her flying
career a few days ago when the motor
Of a plane in which she had started
to Washington from Pittsburgh caught
fire just after taking of.


To friends she admitted that she was
more frightened than she ever had been
in the most perilous portions Of her
own flights.


She was making the flight to Wash
ington in commercial plane when the
center motor broke into flames. TAX
ing turns at the controls, the pilot and
co-pilot fought the flames with hand
extinguisher, leaning out the windows
of the control cabin, first on one side
and then the other.


After subduing the flames the pilot
returned to Pittsburgh and landed
safely without serious damage to the
plane and no injury whatever to his
famous passenger except to her nerves.


Miss Earhart boarded another plane
and completed her flight to Washington.

THE SAIL FISH CLUB, PALM
BEACH, Fla. December 3l.-President
Hooyer's angling luck held good today
with two more hard fighting sail fish
falling early prey as he continued his
search for more finny prizes In the
open Atlantic off Palm Beach.


Setting out half hour after day.
break aboard the small auxiliary s.oop
Orca, the President had his first rike
before am, and landed his sail fish
after 45-minute' struggle. Later he
hooked another and succeeded in
bringing 1t aboard ship.


Fishing conditions were more favor
able today than yesterday. when the
Chief Executive caught three sail fish
and a small dolphin. During much of
the day the sea was as calm as the
Lake Worth anchorage harboring the
U. S. s. Sequoia and other boats Of the
presidential cruising feet. Yesterday
all members of the Hoover party were
tossed about by rolling waves


With his enthusiasm at high pitch
after his mornings luck, Mr.. Hoover
Cancelled arrangements to come in
shore for luncheon and continued his
fishing into the afternoon. Tonight
probably will see the end of his angling
while holding the presidency, for he
has made no plans for fishing tomor-
row and may return northward before
again wetting a line.


The ladies of the presidential party
did not accompany their husbands this
morning as they did yesterday. Mrs.
Hoover, however, accepted an invitation
to use a privately owned motor boat
during the afternoon.


Justice Stone of the Supreme Court
changed places with Senator Austin of
Vermont this morning aboard the Orca,
which also carried Lawrence Richey,
White House secretary.

BERLIN, May 16 (P). = Chancellor
Adolf Hitler prepared today for his
momentous pronouncement on disarm-
ament before tomorrow's special Reichs-
tag session by holding confidential
conference with President Paul Won
Hindenburg.


The whole field Of foreign politics
was discussed at the conference, with
special emphasis on the disarmament
issue, which has faced the chancellor
with one Of the most important de-
Cisions Of his career.


Dr. Wilhelm Frick. minister of in
terror and a stanch Nazi, was present
when the chancellor saw the presi-
dent of the Reich. In order to obtain
the latest information from Geneva.
Herr Hitler also conferred with Count
Rudolf Nadolny. the German delegate
10 the Disarmament Conference who
was summoned home for this purpose.


Meanwhile, foreign Office spokes-
man. Indignantly asking whether the
Geneva negotiations did not wish to
kit at the table with Germany, reiter-
kted the German claims to arms
equality.


Extravagant Demands Denied.


Germany demands nothing extrava-
CANT" the spokesman said. "She wants
equal right"


Charging other powers with adver-
tently neglecting their treaty obliga-
tionS which marks relapse into the
times Of Is years ago." the spokesman
asked whether it was of any sense to
shoulder new obligations without 8d-
vance concessions from other countries.


The chancellor at 3 pm. tomorrow
will outline before the reassembled
Reichstag Germany's position in the
face of the deadlock in the World Dis
armament Conference which followed
German disagreement with articles OF
the British disarmament plan.


The situation in Germany was most
tense as government leaders sought to
check the drift which rapidly was
carrying the country into political isola-
ton


Newspapers generally blamed France
for the Geneva impasse and expressed
surprise that the speech last Saturday
night of Vice Chancellor Frank Won
Papen. IN which he compared the pres
ent situation with that existing in 1914,
had received cool foreign reception.


Blames France for Crisis.


The Wolff News Agency subsidiary,
Deutsche Diplomatische Politische Kor-
respondenZ. spoke of ceaseless French
sabotage" and blamed France for the
crisis in the Geneva deliberations The
subsidiary usually reflects official opin-
ion.


Hitler wants no war" the Deutsche
Allgemeine Zeitung declared in belit-
ting talk Of war. "He could not want
it without jeopardizing his life work and
his theology. He wants peace, security,
equality and gradual revision Of the
Versailles treaty."


Never at any time" the news serv-
ice said, has it been possible to ascer-
tain what concrete disarmament meas
ures France intended to carry out, even
If all her security demands were con-
ceded. The pretense today
that the world is waiting for Germany
to show hers is waste of time"

used by some newspapers.

enced a heavy demand for all sorts OF

The twentieth amendment was writ

the country may not know about it om-
cially for some time.


The amendment, advancing to Janu-
ary from March the date for newly
elected members of Congress to take
their seats, and changing the meet
ing dates of Congress, became effective
yesterday when Missouri became the
thirty sixth State to ratify the article.


The Secretary of State will issue a
proclamation when all of the 36 States
that have ratified the amendment no.
tify him of their approval. His procla-
nation, however, will simply declare
the necessary three-fourths of the
States have ratified and the amend
ment became effective on the date on
which the thirty-sixth State acted.


There is no necessity that the Sec
retary notify either the President or
Congress.


His proclamation enumerates the
States that have ratified the amend
ment and his proclamation, along with
the certified copies Of the State ratifi-
cations, goes into the State Department
archives.


The original documents are bound
into big, leather-covered volumes and
stored in guarded rooms in the base
ment of the State Department.

ance."

Chaco battlefront since hostilities were
resumed last July. The Paraguayan
offensive was carried on late last year
after the capture of Fort Boqueron in
September

Saavedra, salient protecting their


headquarters at Fort Munoz, for several


weeks until about month ago. Para


guayanS had closed In both north and


south of Saavedra.


Fort Ayala is about 40 miles east of


Saavedra toward the Paraguyan border.

weakness developed In stocks again to-

tionally higher still under the stimulus

pool operations in this group last Sum-
mer. National Distillers half way

Smelling, up at one time to points,

fererS.

NEW YORK, January 1.-THE motor
industry expresses itself as well pleased
at the attendance and sales made at
the thirty-third annual National Auto
mobile Show here which ends weeks
run tonight.


Attendance UP to Thur ;day night was
below that Of 1882, but the crowds
seeking admission that night and Fri
day blocked traffic on the streets ad-
jacent to Grand Central Palace. Sales

or more we're 800 per cent above such
orders at the 1882 show. Sales of low
priced cars were said to have been
satisfactory, but no figures were given
out.


Aside from the business provided for
decorators, drapery and carpet manu-
facturers, commercial printers and pub
fishers: the hotels benefited largely
from the show Automobile makers
occupied % per cent more display
space in hotels during the current ex-
hibit than they did year ego.


Wall Street, throughout the expo
sition heard conflicting reports about
attendance, sales and models. The
present show, in point of money
expended, in decorations and models,
was the most costly in the his
tory of the industry. Some tech
nicians termed it the most inter-
esting show. Portions of the public
praised it as the most beautiful. Women
generally agreed that the new color

ernistic designs.

SALT LAKE CITY, Utah, October

October 30. Generally. many Of the
hunters get deer and are through the
first day, as one buck each Is the limit.

mountains, where the deer like to

snow falls soon, the kill will be light,
despite the fact that the number Of
hunters swarming over the hills has
been unusually large.

dinarily interesting events have failed

ocratic and Republican leaders and many

have been brave enough to say they

BALTIMORE, Oct. 11.-Movie
scenario writer's missed a choice
opportunity for an idea" yester-
day, when drama was portrayed
in case presented in Judge Rob
ert F. Stanton's court here.


Mrs. Ida Crosby was suing her
husband, Charles Crosby, for non.
support, but Crosby contended he
could not be sued because Mrs.
CroSby's first husband, from
whom she never had been di-
vorced, is alive.


The drama" began, according
to testimony, with the marriage
of Mrs. Crosby to Robert Johnson
in 1901. In 1916 johnson disap-
peared and was not heard from
for 10 years.


Buried Wrong Man


In 1925, Mrs. johnson read in .
newspaper that Robert johnson
was i'll in hospital and she went
to see him. The patient said his
wife's name was Ida and spoke
intimately of the family but when
she asked him if he recognized
her he only turned away The
next day the patient died, but not
before Mrs. Johnson's daughter,
Ruth, had seen him and ldenti-
fled him as her father.


So Mrs. johnson collected $500
life insurance for his death and
buried the man in a cemetery
here. A priest also said he, too,
believed the dead man was her
husband.


Real Johnson Returned


In 1880 Mrs. johnson married
Crosby, and four months later,
the real Robert Johnson returned,
but said he would not contest
her marriage to Crosby since the
latter was better able to support
her than he. Crosby, informed
Of Johnson's return, said his wife
must choose between the two
men, and Mrs. Crosby chose him.
Johnson left for Florida, and
Ruth Johnson, his daughter, has
been corresponding with him
there since.


A month ago Mr.. and Mrs.
Crosby separated.


Judge Stanton dismissed the
non-support charge, advising the
couple to live apart until they
could obtain counsel to determine
their marital status.

HAVANA, February 24-Eight bombs
were exploded in Havana within two
hours after midnight today as the
thirty eighth Cuban independence day
began.


Meanwhile the capital was scanning
reports anxiouSly to determine whether
rumored revolutionary movement was
taking form. Mexico City dispatches
recently predicted that movement OF
rebels from the mainland toward Cuba
would coincide with bombings in Ha-
vana.


Three of the bombs which exploded
early today were large ones, while the
five others, which were smaller, caused
several hundred persons to desert the
ball room at the Centro Asturiano.


Reports from Camaguey and Santiago
said those cities were quiet. However
unconflrmed rumorS said rebels were
numerous around Cienfuegos and that
tense situation prevailed at NuevitaS
Communications were interrupted east
of this city.


A Santiago dispatch said the Jibacoa
Sugar Mill, near Manzanilla, was de-
stroyed by fire yesterday afternoon, but
that the cause of the fire had not been
determined.


Bartolome Mas was arrested after
the bombing of the ball room. Police
said they found fire bombs in his
pocket.


Cuban Independence day dates from
February "a, 1895, when band of
Cuban patriots rose in arms at the
little town. of Baire. After three years
of conflict with the Spanish the United
States took a hand in the situation.

MEMPHIS. January 5-Cap'n G.
Peters Lee-the last of the steamboatin'
Lees-died at his river home yesterday
near the gaunt old Mississippi, which
the Lee packets have travelled since
1862.


He was 81 and had been steamboat
master since he was 25.


Some of the greatest boats on the
river have flown the Lee ensign. Most
of them were designed by Cap'n Peters
Lee. The James Lee was the first
packet of the line. Then the Robert E.
Lee (not the racer), the Bob Lee Geor-
gia Lee. Reese Lee, Sadie Lee, Stacker
Lee. Peters Lee and the last, James Lee.


Cap'n Peters-tfrats what river folks
called hinl-Was the last connection be-
tween the Mississippi and the Lees.
And now for the first time since his
grandfather established the Lee Lines
in 1852 and ran supplies to the Con-
federates, there are no Lees on the
river.


There was an affinity between the
Cap'n and the Mississippi which was
quite beyond the ken of landlubbers. He
ron boat during the glamorouS days
of river travel when pilots fed fat meat
to their boilers to get more steam.


Everybody of the river clans knew
the Cap'n. He was friend to rousta-
bouts, levee Negroes, little boys and
dogs. One hound was at his feet con-
stantly for almost IA years.


They still sing songs in the bayou
country about the exploits of the James
Lee-the queen of the line. 1t was as
famous down here as the City of Nat
chez.


The Lee whistleAa melodious thing
that howled for channel rights, and got
them-was on the first James Lee.
That whistle has become symbol down
here. It was transferred to the second
and third James Lees and later was
perched near the towering stacks of
the Harry Lee.


Last night the Harry Lee worked the
bends of the White River. in the gumbo
lands of Arkansas, and the Lee whistle
still hoWled for channel rights. The
blasts are hoarse and deep, but they are
lullaby for steanboatin' men.

BERLIN, February A Telegraphen
Union dispatch from Bucharest tonight
quoted Nicholas Titulescu, Rumanian
foreign minister, as saying a martial
law decree already has been signed by
King Carol and will be put into effect
tomorrow morning in Bucharest, the
Ploesti oil fields and four smaller cities.


The aim Of the action, the dispatch
said, is to preserve order in the coun-
try. The foreign minister was said to
have asserted that foreign countries
need have no fears about Rumania's
stability and that Rumania can deal
with the situation.


Acts Against Agitation.


The Rumanian government last night
was empowered to declare martial law
in an effort to curb unrest and agita-
ton.


officials said the measure was neces-
sary because of recent riots in the
Ploesti oil district, when several hun
dred employees wrecked the interior Of
an oil refinery building. and because
of student disorders, allegedly involving
FaScistS.


The Telegraphen Union reported that
despite the martial law order, several
political meetings were scheduled for
Sunday. and, as was known tonight,
they will be held.


The agency further said that railroad
workers were the target for agitators
who sought to have them declare q
strike.


Publication Today.


The Wolff (German) News Agency
also in a dispatch from Bucharest said
the decree would be published tomorrow
and would be effective Immediately on
publication.


Meanwhile the government planned to
issue an appeal tomorrow to all citizens
to preserve order.


The Wolff correspondent said the de-
cree would affect Bucharest, the Ploesti
oil fields, GalatZ, Temesvar, CZernowitz
and the Prohoba industrial district.

Surely" you say, "she must
have been an unnatural mon
ster. Thank God, people like
that don't live today!"


But you're wrong. She wasn't
an unnatural monster. And peo-
pie like that do live today-live
right on your block, in your
office, perhaps right in your
own house.


There's a book you should
read. It's the biography of
Marie Antoinette by Stefan
zweig. Most biographies of the
great make Indifferent reading,
because their characters are so
far outside our daily life that
they seem unreal as fairy tales.
But Stefan Zweig gives you
Marie Antoinette just as she
was-a gay, lazy, aimless, warm
hearted, empty-headed little
creature whose like you meet
every day in the beauty shop or
across the bridge table.


Poor butterfly! Never in all
her silly days did she have one
really cruel desire. Suffering
shocked her exactly as much as
it would you or me.


Yet she let her people live in
abject misery!


Yes, but she didn't want them
to be miserable. She just didn't
see their misery; that was all.
Daily she passed by it, smiling,
nodding, blowing kisses from
her rosy little mouth with her
foolish little hands. And, as
she passed, her jeweled skirts
brushed their filthy rags. Yet
she never saw them because


SHE SAW ONLY THAT
WHICH SHE WISHED TO
SEE; BELIEVED ONLY THAT
WHICH SHE WISHED TO
BELIEVE. AND SHE DID NOT
WISH TO SEE OR BELIEVE

ANYTHING WHICH WOULD
MAKE HER FEEL PERSON.
ALLY UNCOMFORTABLE OR
RESPONSIBLE. Says Stefan
Zweig:


"The world that lay beyond
the narrow circle within which
the nobility moved was for her
practically non-existent. Not q
notion had she that round the
opera house of Paris there
stretched a gigantic town, filled
with poverty and discomfort:
that beyond the ponds Of Tria'
non, well-stocked with manda-
rim ducks and overfed swans, be-
yond the lawns on which the
peacocks Haunted their plumes
the peasants houses were fall
ing into ruins and the barns
were empty. She never knew
that millions upon millions of
the French people toiled and
hungered, alternating between
44ODC d41u OCoPdAA'


Why was pretty, playful Ma.
rie Antoinette's life so shame
full; her death so dreadful?
That was why. She was not a
monster, yet her record was
mons trous, because SHE
WOULD NOT FACE THE
REALITY of 1893. And So
they punished her.


So, presently, many excellent,
law-abiding, harmless" citizens
of these United States may be
punished-unless they get busy
and face the grim reality of
1888. They may not lose their
heads-but they may have their
smugness and feelings consid-
erably shaken.


THERE ARE STARVING
PEOPLE IN AMERICA TODAY.
THERE ARE MILLIONS OF
AMERICANS AS HUNGRY, DIS
EASED AND DESPERATE AS
THOSE FRANTIC FRENCH
PEASANTS WHO GUILLO-
TINED THEIR QUEEN.


They are hungry, diseased
and desperate for exactly the
same reason. Those who should
realize their plight and help
them refuse to see it, or ad-
nit that it. exists.


"All this talk about a revo-
lution-it's absurd" they laugh,
shuffling the cards. lighting
their cigars. with fat, jeweled
fingers. "Of course times have
been hard. Look at all we
lost in the market crash! But
these horrors you hear about
they're just talk. Why, most Of
those men in the bread line
wouldn't take a job if you
gave them one. And as far
starving-with all this charity
poor people are eating better
than they ever did before"


That's what these excellent
law-abiding. harmless" Amer
ican citizens are saying, and
honestly believing these days.
That's what Marie Antoinette

SUMTER. 8. c., August 21.-Some-

duction figures probably will have to be
revised, for G. c. Rowland, Sumter
banker, has developed flve-lock-boll
cotton to take the place Of the usual
four -lock-boel.


In addition, the new type is an early
and blight proof variety and weighs
approximately 80 per cent more than
the common staple.
Like a romance is the flve-year story
of Rowland's painstaking efforts to pro-
duce the new type which, he says, pro-
duces more cotton for the same amount
of work and fertilizer.


Rowland, who has combined farming
with his banking duties, first noticed a
ive-lock-boll OF cotton five years ago
while walking through one of his fields.
After considerable effort he located sew
eral more He offered pickers a pre-
MUM for such bolls and finally obtained
quite number


During the Winter, Rowland and his
family picked the seed by hand. and
the next season these selected seed were
planted and the crop again carefully
handpicked for the five-lock-bolls.
Again and again the process was re-
peated


This year Rowland had sufficient seed
culled from his experimental fields to
plant so acres. Already over bale to
the acre had developed before boil wee
wills arrived and now pickers are going
through this field, picking only five
lock-bolls which total about IS per cent
of the crop.


The bolls are larger and fluffier than
ordinary cotton and Rowland expects to
gather between 40 and so bales from
this type.

ing the first half Of this year. 1t said

AUBURNDALE, Mass, March ALL
commodities recorded moderate down.
ward trend during the past week. Six
out Of IA groups were slightly lower,
seven remained unchanged, and only
one group successfully advanced. Al
though there were numerous price
changes downward, the magnitude OF
the concession was extremely small ana
as q result the total decline was not
radical, particularly in view Of gen.
eral conditions. The state Of industry
failed to improve, while financial con-
ditions were badly demoralized as 81
States took definite action to meet the
banking crisis. The moratorium and
holiday movement spread from the
Central States to the Pacific Coast.
More emergency laws have been passed
and drastic measures are contemplated.
Ordinarily such a condition would force
fully affect commodity prices, but be-
cause deflation Is so complete, the ac-
tual decline in the price level was only
fractional-about the degree that would
ordinarily be expected even though no
critical financial crisis existed.


Industrial Prices.


Industrial prices held steady showing
practically no change. The normal sea-
sonal decline in industrial activity Is
subject to some extension because OF
the banking situation. In no instance
has there been any sign OF panic
and 1t is generally agreed that the
financial system is sound and will with
out any difficulty bridge this crisis
without causing anv serious menace
forcing industrial activity to materially
lower levels or causing any unusual
break in commodity prices


Agricultural products showed more
weakness than any other group al
though the decline was not as sharp as
was the case after the turn of the year.
Agitation for farm relief has not les
sened, but the clamoring for artificial
ways and means has lost power. The
decline in the agricultural price index
during the past week was due to the
following items: Wheat, corn, oats,
WOOL f1axseed and butter.


Live stock prices represented another
group that declined quite sharply dur
ing the past week rejecting a reaction
In hog prices. following sharp ad-
vance, and lower quotations for cattle.


Non-ferrous metals represent the only
group to advance, due principally to
two commodities-tin and zinc. The
six commodity groups that we're lower
during the past week were industrial
and agricultural products, live stock,
fuels, hides and leather and fine tex
tiles The index figure for building
materials, chemicals, ferrous metals

The Supreme Court held today that
Congress could not reduce the salaries
of judges of the District of Columbia
Supreme Court and District Court of
Appeals during their service on the
bench.


The crux Of the ruling was that the
courts were created by the Constitu-
ton and were not legislative courts
created by Congress. The judges in
volved had declared their willingness
voluntarily to contribute their utmost
during the depression in the spirit of
the provisions of the economy act but
they had insisted-and their contention
was upheld-that their salaries could
not be reduced for the period for which
they were appointed


Chief Justice Hughes and Justices
Van Devanter and Cardozo dissented.
The Chief Justice said the Congress
had power at its pleasure to change
the tenure of the judges of both courts
and could at any time, II 1t desired,
reduce their salaries.


Most Federal judges, under the in
depreciation that they we're members
Of constitutional courts not created by
Congress, were exempt from the pro-
visions of last years economy act,
slashing the salaries of most Govern
ment employees and Office holders. Only
three or four voluntarily returned to
the Treasury the amount that would
have been deducted had Congress been
enabled to slash their pay.

BOISE, Idaho, August 26-Concerted

panies led the fight for tax slashes.

erty was still being assessed at over

farm lands had been granted sizeable
decreases.


The power companies contended that
unless their assessments were reduced
they would be forced to cut their pay
rolls and thereby materially retard the
N. r. A. program in Idaho.


Utilities have paid 100 per cent of
their assessments. it was declared.
while real property taxes are SIS per
cent delinquent. This delinquency, the
utilities pointed out. throws a still
heavier burden on public utilities by
denying them what they term Just"
reductions.

GUAYAQUIL, Ecuador, Nov. "a
uN.S).-Another weird chapter
IN the life of the Baroness Eloissa
Bousquet De Wagner, self-styled
"Queen of the Galapagos" came
to light here today with the reve'
1ation that she and her lawless
band of courtiers cast away in
0 small boat a pair of young
newlyweds who sought refuge on
her island after a shipwreck.


The victims we're Pablo Rolando,
Of the town of Esmeraldas. and
his bride, the former Blanca
Rosa Fernandez.


Picked Up At Sea


They drifted for several days
In an open boat, and were finally
picked up by the clipper ship
Fortune, bound to Ecuador from
the Galapagos Islands.


The baroness decree banishing
them to the mercy of the sea
was the first heard OF this
extraordinary woman since the
disclosure some months ago that
she had set herself up as queen"
OF Floreana Island, one OF the
sparsely inhabited territories IN
the Galapagos group.


Pablo Rolando and his VIE
were passengers on a honeymoon
trip aboard the sailing yacht
Santa Rosa. Several miles OIL
the Galapagos Islands, the vessel
was overtaken by a storm, and
al aboard took to the boats.


Thrown Into Jail


The five survivors were taken
before the baroness after being
bound hand and foot, and were
thrown into prison.


For three days they were held
and then hailed again before the
ruler of the island. She told them
she neither was able nor desired
to offer them hospitality and sug-
gested that all depart instantly
for some other port.


The queen commanded that the
Seamen travel in one boat and the
newlyweds in another.


She explained with a laugh that
this would afford the honeymoon.
ing couple a better opportunity
for romance. So that nothing
might interfere with love-making,
she added, she deprived them Of
food and water and ordered them
set adrift with but one oar.


Wife Attacked


Far of fthe coast, the sailors
rowed abreast of Rolando's craft
and attempted to throw the hus-
band overheard and attack his
wife. Rolando drew pistol and
fired into the midst of the at
tackers. All three fell into the
sea and the couple resumed their
voyage alone.


It was several days later that
the ship Fortune happened across
their path and rescued the couple,
suffering from exhaustion and ex
posure and on the verge of star
walton.

Ambassador Oscar Cintas Of
Cuba conferred for an hour and a
half today with Secretary Hull
and other State Department Off
cials about the situation in his
island republic and later said he
had come to report on his con-
ference yesterday with President
Roosevelt at Hyde Park.


Appearing somewhat excited,
the representative of the Ma
chado government also con-
ferred with Undersecretary Phil
ips and Assistant Secretary
Caffrey. Cintas told newspaper
men that only economic matters
had been discussed.


There was a rumor, however,
that the Ambassador had con-
veyed to the Secretary of State
the reaction of President Machado
to the plan for his retirement
submitted by Ambassador Sumner
Welles in Havana.


Undersecretary Phillips said later the
Ambassador did not bring any reply
from Machado to the appeal which
President Roosevelt made to him yes
terday for betterment on the Cuban
situation


Phillips added that the discussion
was largely economic, although the
political questions also were considered


The Ambassador himself said he had
no reports of the political situation
this morning from Havana and added
that his talk with President Roosevelt
yesterday had concerned economic
questions.


The Undersecretary expressed hope
that mediation will settle the Cuban
difficulties and said that conferences
were going on constantly in Havana

BOSTON, April 8.-In an analysis Of
trends of the 60 leading industries of the
country, the United Business Service
concludes that in 80 important lines
volumes are running close to a year ago,
indicating definite resistance to further
deflation. The firmness Of the trends
in these industries shows the beneficial
effects of the courageous adjustments
that have been made in operating and
overhead costs.


The 80 industries with stable trends
follow: Aircraft, apparel. automobiles,
baking. bread; baking speciality; can
ming, chain stores, chemicals, cigarettes,
coal, anthracite; coal. bituminous; cot
ton goods, dairy products, electric light
and power, -four milling, leather, lum-
Der. meat packing package foods, paper,
petroleum, producing; petroleum, refin-
ing; printing. railroad equipment, rayon,
shoes, silks, sugar refining, woolens and
zinc


In every depression, the service points
out. there is natural point at which
the liquidation from the preceding ex-
pansion halts. Activity has been cur
tailed more and more as prices have
dropped. Today's prices are so low that
many producers have shut down-others
are operating at extremely low levels.
Such condition never remains long.
Consumption has been larger than pro-
duction-stocks of manufactured goods
now aggregate 8 per cent under last
year, and % per cent under 1929. ThiI
inventory vacuum must be filled, say
the review.

Overrun by Ahen Ghosts.

Closing her second successful Winter,
the Old Woman Who Lives in a Shoe
was represented on the air last night
IN two appeals for jobs for the four un-
employed men who have helped dis
tribute 10000 pairs of shoes to the
jobless during the cold months


Vernon West, assistant corporation
counsel, pleaded for employment for the
four men. who have worked the Whole
season without remuneration. At $50
O'Clock Mrs. Ruth Bryan Owen, former
Representative from Florida, repeated
the appeal. All four men are chauffeurs.


Today the Old Woman closed her
headquarters at 727 Seventeenth street
until next Fall. In distributing the
10000 pairs of shoes this season the
organization has functioned without ap-
pealing for funds. depending solely on
the generosity of the public.


Old shoes sent in for distribution
have been repaired without cost by the
William Hahn Shoe Co., while other
merchants and business men have do
mated services, including rent for the
headquarters. haulage and fuel.


Regis Noel, local attorney, is chair
man of the committee in charge, while
Lawrence F. Schmeckebier is vice chair
man; George E. Fleming. treasurer, and
George Emerson, secretary.

Big radio stations have started a new
drive for licenses to use the maximum
power Of $4,000 watts. Five stations
have filed with the Federal Radio Com
mission applications for authority to
increase their outputs, but in every in
stance it Is likely that the commission
will defer action until late this year or
next year.


The five stations are: WGN and
WMAQ, Chicago; WBz. Boston; WBAL,
Baltimore, and WHAM, Rochester,
N. Y. Each operates on clear chan
mel Commission regulations, however.
prescribe that only one-half of the 40
clear channels available shall be per-
mitted to use the maximum power, and
it already has made such authorizations
on 20 of the waves.


These new applications may result In
a repetition Of the free -for-an battle
over high power staged before the
commission three years ago, eliminating
in court actions which were dismissed
only few months ago. Two dozen sta
tions on clear channels then applied for
the nine vacant 50,000-watt positions.
Most Of the stations that were turned
down took legal action, but one by one
they dropped out until the final case
was dismissed this Spring.

While most American railroads
strangely lag behind, practically all OF
the larger countries Of Europe now have
equipped their passenger trains for radio
reception.


Latest to inaugurate the "hsten-while-
you travel system is Great Britain
which has equipped a number OF its
express trains with head sets. Canada
first discovered the advantages Of train
radio with receivers or headphone out
fits.


Since then Russia, Germany, France
and England have followed suit, while
trains running through many Of the
smaller European countries also offer
radio service.


While some OF the crack trains In
this country operating in the West and
South are equipped with radio receiv-
ers in their club cars, the big railroads
of the East have disdained radio. Sew
eral years ago the Pennsylvania, Balti-
more g. Ohio and New York Central
were openly criticized for failure TO pro-
vide radio facilities.


At that time the roads claimed 1t
was technically not feasible to pick up
programs with any degree OF quality
aboard moving trains. Since then, how
ever, according to engineers, the strides
made in shielding sets and with auto
matte volume control make the use OF
radio entirely satisfactory, although
some fading naturally is occasioned.

NEW YORK, April 29.-The Senate's
acceptance of the inflation-a agricultural
hrl set the signal for fresh frenzy OF
buying in the Stock Exchange TODAY,
sending many issues up to more than
5 points, in the biggest Saturdays trad
ing In many months. The market closed
buoyantly, with turnover for the two
hour session of some 100000 shares.


Traders who had put out short lines
In expectation Of sharp technical reac-
ton were severely squeezed in the new
uprush, and wide assortment Of issues
reached the best levels for the year or
longer. Price averages were boosted to
the highest level since last September.


Trade News Favorable.


Further indications Of business expan-
sion IN the week end trade reviews was
also undoubtedly factor in the up
surge. Reports from the steel and auto
mobile industries were particularly en-
couraging. Further stiffening in steel
prices was indicated, and estimates in
dicated that ingot production had
stepped up to new high levels for more
than year.


Trading facilities were again over
whelmed by the rush of business in the
Stock Exchange, and the ticker ran for
several minutes after the close.


American Can jumped several points
in what looked Like a short squeeze.
Issues up to included United States
Steel common, American Telephone,
Union Pacific, American Tobacco B,
Corn Products Case, Western Union and
United States Steel preferred. Buying
was well distributed throughout the
major groups. Mail order and farm i'm
plement issues were buoyant. Motors
were particularly active, with General
Motors, Nash and Chrysler up around
point. Issues up about included Santa
Fe, New York Central, National Steel,
American Smelling, Montgomery Ward,
Sears, Roebuck, International Harvester.
Westinghouse Electric and others.


Commodities were buoyant as weh,
and second-grade bends scared. The
weekly freight car loadings showed
check to the recent advance, but rail-
road quarters looked for further fxpan-
sion. For the week ended April %,
class roads handled 1929 cars, or
1,245 less than in the previous week.


Dollar Weakens.


Sears, Roebuck's sales report for the
four weeks ended April % showed a re-
duction of only 12.4 per cent from 1882,
against a drop Of 1873 per cent for the
first IL weeks of the year.


Cotton jumped about 50 a bale, and
wheat advanced 2 to cents in the
earlier trading. Foreign exchanges
again strengthened against the dollar,
with sterling up several cents, and
French francs up several points, al
though failing to reach their recent
highs.

NEW YORK. March 4.-The Eastern
~ intercollegiate Basket Ball League


all but winds up its 1888 cam
paign tonight with three-game sched-
ule, bringing every team in the circuit
into action.


The most important contests, from a
championship angle, will be played in
New Haven and Princeton At New
Haven the pace-setting Yale outfit
tackles Cornell, while at Princeton the
Tigers will seek to repel the Dartmouth
Indians. The third game, at Philadel-
phia. involves Columbia and Pennsyl-
vania.


After these three games have been
played only two more will be left or
the regular schedule. Dartmouth will
face Columbia at New York on Mon
day and Princeton will play Penn at
Philadelphia a week from tonight.


A victory for Yale over Cornell au-
tomatically will clinch at least a tie for
the title for the Ellis even should Prince
ton win from both Dartmouth and
Penn. In that event Yale and Prince
ton would wind up the season in a
deadlock for first place, necessitating a
playof for the championship now held
by the Tigers.

Eastern Intercollegiate Basket Ball Con-
ference season at Philadelphia tonight
in game with the league leading Pitt
Panthers. A victory for Temple will
give the owls the lead and at least a
tie for the title. Pitt leads with four
victories and one defeat, as against

all are in the running for the cham

BY the Associated Press.


OSLO, Norway, October 16.-Candi-
dates of 18 parties participated today
in the first general elections in Norway
in three years.


A new party in the field is the
National Union party, whose leader is
Mai. Vidkun Quisling, former cabinet
member, who has been described as
"Norway's strong man" and "Norway's
Hitler"


Mai. Quisling has directed vigorous
attack against the Labor and Com
munist parties. His entry into today's
election resulted in a split in the three
dominant parties. and in consequence
there was some likelihood that the
Labor party-the fourth large group
might benefit.


The Conservatives and Agrarians have
been fighting the Liberals, charging
them with having betrayed the united
front" which was so successful against
the Labor party in the last election.

BALTIMORE, August 9.-Dr. j. Knox
Insley, Maryland commissioner Of LABOR
and statistics, reported yesterday that
factory employment in the Baltimore
area increased 9.7 per cent during the
month ending July is and factory pay
rolls during the same period increased
141 per cent.


These increases, he said. reflect the
upward surge in both jobs and wages
that began about March. Since that
time, he said, each succeeding month
has shown increases over the preceding
month.


The employment increase for the
month ending June is was l.9 per cent
and the pay roll increase 8.5 per cent.


At the same time DR.. Insley's report
was made, a statement from the Balti-
more Emergency Relief Commission
showed decrease in the number of
Baltimore families receiving care from
welfare agencies.

fare care here last week was 23,580, a

approximately 300 families have been

communication.

sweeping tide which accompanied
the storm were later rescued by

MADRID, January "a wave of Ex-

young republic of Spain left a toll

Der wounded today while an unesti-
mated number were under arrest.


Striking suddenly and without warn

tions apparently were operating under
a coordinate command. The attacks
occurred mainly in industrial centers
of the country through the day Sunday
and last night.


From OViedo, in the northwest.
where striking mine workers killed ar
electrical engineer while he was going
home, the outbreaks carried through
Salient, where a civil guard was killed.
and on to Lerida and Barcelona, with
seven killed in each of the latter two
northeast cities.


All Troops Called Out.


Salient is near the textile center

bellion occurred in January, 1881, Just
three months before the republic was
proclaimed.


All armed forces were called out to
cope with the uprisings. Scores of
Extremists and Communist were i'm

last August, and Communists were re-

1t was estimated that 35 persons

and three militiamen

Extremists in Madrid and in Cara
banchel, where Syndicalists attempted
to storm a barracks. One person was
wounded and IL arrested. There were
reports of attempts to storm barracks
and police stations in other cities


AT Lerida, capital of the province of

Castillo Barracks, but were repealed.


Police Charge Crowds.


Police charged and dispersed crowds
at the Arch of Triumph in Barcelona.
More than 100 Extremists attacked the
France Railroad Station, throwing
bombs, but were quickly driven away by
civil guards. Shooting broke out be-
tween the Extremists and guards at
San Augustin Barracks and in front
Oh the Palace OF justice.


officials said the uprising had been
planned for several weeks and that
stores of arms and bombs had been
seized. Armed guards were placed
around police headquarters in Madrid,
Barcelona and other cities long before

said today they believed the movement
was collapsing.


Apart from frustrated attempts to as
sault the artillery barracks and Quatro

ministry and official buildings in

nists who placed authorities and civil
guards in Jail and raised a red ana
black flag over the city hall. Rein
fcrcements of civil guards and assault
guards recaptured the city after u
battle.


One civil guard and one townsman
we're killed and several wounded.


Extraordinary precautions were taken
to avoid further trouble in the region

the "crystallization of American and

America thereby obtained naval su-

WILKES-BARRE, Pa. May 26
G.N.sD.-A detail of 18 mounted
State policemen, resorting to tear
gas and clubs, drove nearly a
thousand men, women and chill
dren today from the vicinity of
the West End Coal Company
operation at Mocanaqua.


Detailed to the scene at day.
break, the troopers found nearly
the entire town out in protest
against the practice of the COM
pany in working strippings and a
culm bank with foremen and
other officials while regular mine
workers are idle.


Witnesses said the troopers
drove their horses into the crowds
and used clubs freely. One
mounted officer snatched up an
American flag around which a
group had rallied. Several women
tainted and others were reported
to have been injured slightly.

the storm from a sister freighter, the

being towcd py the rescue ship when
the line broke. Its position was about
120 miles east of Sable Island.

er, was bound for New York and Phil
adelphia when the propeller was lost.
It sent out distress call early Monday,
when $50 miles south Of Cape Race, and

dalusia from Jamaica. Others we're

Garden makers who rent their
homes and therefore do not feel
like investing in shrubs or peren-
mails will find the spider plant,
or Cleome pungens, useful, because
it grows tall enough to act as
substitute for shrubbery. The
growth is rapid, too, and the
flowers persist until the coming
of Fall. Then they are likely
to self-sow and come up freely
the next year. The plants grow
best in rather rich soil, and
should stand one foot apart.


The common name Of spider
plant was given because the long
stamens and the curious seed
pods suggest q 1ong-legged spider.
The blossoms are curiously sticky
when touched. They are not
very attractive in the middle Of
the day, as they partially close
then, but when evening comes
they open to their fullest extent
and make q very pretty appear
ance, being deep rose in color.

Naming basketball first, the

Coach Mesmer was ready with

He's decided that Ed Hargaden

There's nothing like a good

spacious Brookland floor. The
first team lined up with Abe
Rosenfield and Babe Gearty, for
wards; Bernie Lieb, center; and
Gene Augusterfer and Eddie

the Cardinal ringmen and deliy-

passing" against Baxter, who

SHREVEPORT, La, April l
GN.S0.-Torhadoes which in the
past SO hours have hurled death
and destruction across four
States left q known death list Of
10 persons today in addition to
hundreds Of injured and stagger-
ing property damage.


Originating in the East Texas
numbering region, the winds
swept northeastward into Louisi-
ana, touched Southern Arkansas.
and then whirled into Mississippi,
where villages and rural commu-
mites were uprooted and 40 per-
sons were killed. The larger
cities were spared.


Flood Peril Grows


Torrential rains that accom-
panied the tornadoes swelled
creeks and rivers in Louisiana,
Mississippi and Texas, creating
a flood menace that threatened
to bring further devastation to
the plantation and numbering ter
ritory of the deep South.


The rains made by-roads nearly
impossible, crippling relief work,
which was directed by Red Cross
officials.


The tentative death toll by
States:


Mississippi, 40.


Texas, 20.


Louisiana, g..


Arkansas, !.


Hundreds of persons, many OF
them negroes, we're injured as the
winds threw their houses and
huts down upon them. Tempo
rarily isolated by bad roads, many
of the injured waited for hours
before relief could reach them.


Into Delta Lands


Rescue workers were still ex-
periencing difficulty in reaching
rural communities in Louisiana
and Mississippi where the storm
had touched.


The first tornado, after sweep
ing east Texas, crossed the Mis-
sissippi River Thursday and
whipped into the delta lands and
then into the plantation area,
killing nine persons before dipping
southwark. At Brookhaven it
killed two women.


Whirling next into the lumber
ing region, the storm killed IA
residents of the village of San
derson, and eight persons in Har-
mony.


Crop Damage Heavy


Visiting Alabama, the high
winds did some damage at Brew
ton, near Pensacola, Fla, and in
jured 80 persons.


Along the entire path of the
tornadoes rain fell in sheets, do
ing extensive damage to crops.


The winds were felt as far
north as Chattanooga, where some
property damage was done.

Pin Oak.


Quercus palustris.


TN Eastern United States, the pin oak


is the most important and attrac-


tive oak. In their youth the trees
1 are easily recognized from some


distance and picked out from
among neighboring trees. The trunk Is
continuous, not dividing as Is the prac-
tice Of most oaks. The lateral branches
are slender and short, while the lower
ones droop, often touching the ground.
The upper ones point almost straight
skyward and those along the middle OF
the trunk extend at right angles from
the main stem.


With this three-way branch habit, the
pin oak Is a conspicuous figure among
its associates. As the tree grows older
the lower branches drop of or hang
like dead stubs. Its name is derived
from the presence Of pin-like twigs set
all over its branches.


The leaves look very much like those
Of the scarlet oak, but are neither so
glossy nor SO fine grained. They are
from 8 to S 1ncheS long and to 9
lobed, with bristle-like point at the
tip. All Summer they are a bright.
beautiful grsen, and in the Autumn
they become a deep rich scarlet. They
do not drop off like the leaves OF other
oaks, but remain on for several seasons
and for this reason the tree has been
mentioned as the evergreen oak.

getting fully acquainted with this tree
Is its exceedingly small acorns. They

The man reported to have caused
the fire took one frightened look at the
scene then left hurridly, according to
Joseph Messick, IS years old, Of 1887
Tenth street, a bystander.


Tank Torn Open.


The collision occurred shortly before
8 o'clock. The bus, from Hyattsville,
was headed south on Tenth street, and
the truck belonging to the Terminal
Ice & Fuel Co., was bound east on o
street. They met virtually head-on.
and the gasoline tank under the front
Of the bus was torn open. The bus
was damaged otherwise, as was the
truck.


McCracken pulled into the curb and
discharged his passengers, and spec
tators sensing the danger from the
flowing gasoline, shouted warnings
against lighting matches.
Young Messick, however, reported
that midd1e-aged man who ran up
to the scene about 5 minutes after the
collision lighted a cigarette as he came
and dropped the match. Instantly the
flames shot up and began to spread
wherever the gas had fallen.


The automobile destroyed was an old
model Ford coupe bearing Virginia license
159-288. The owners Of two of the other
cars damaged were at the wreck They
were John Day, 1882 Tenth street, and
Floyd Hackney, 1889 Duncan street
northeast. The other car damaged, q
Chrysler coach, bears District tags
P-1987, listed to Lillian Heller, 1900
block of Eleventh street.


Other Buses Arrive.
Just as the fire started another
Washington Railway & Electric bus
came up. bound north, and another
south. The northbound bus was IN
the path of the flames and the driver
from the other, seeing his predicament,
went to his assistance with fire ex-
tinguisher. The help was insufficient,
however, and the northbound bus,
forced to 60 ahead, plunged safely
through the ring of flames.
Meanwhile IRE apparatus was called
and put out the ire before It had q
chance to spread beyond the line Of
parked cars.


Robert Fleming, colored, SO, 200
block Of K street, the truck driver, vas
held for investigation at the second
precinct.

PARIS, March 21.-Former Premier

debts due the United States and Leon
Blum, Socialist Deputy, upheld the
Chambers decision Of last December
not to pay in meetings today Of the two
major parties of the governments ma
jority.


NJ Herriot, who talked with Premier
Edouard Daladier this morning, after
telling Radical Socialist party group
that payment should be made, said he
would take no initiative because his
own government was overthrown on the
question last December. He emphasized,
however, "the necessity Of voting pay
ment without delay"


M. Blum meanwhile told the Socialists
they should adhere to the Chambers
refusal until the government had been
assured that President Roosevelt's atti-
tude fulfilled the Chambers condition
for . general conference Of creditors
and debtors.


The Socialists sent emissaries to ask
the government concerning the present
status Of the matter.

just to be sure that her proposition would
