BY the Associated Press.


PHILADELPHIA, August :l.-Two
men were killed and at least eighteen
persons were injured today as 200 police
battled many times their number OF
strikers and sympathizers outside the
Cambria Hosiery Mills. Northeastern
Philadelphia.


The dead men were Glen H. Norwood
and Frank Minor, strike pickets. The
shooting occurred after the overturning
of truck which was bringing non-
strikers to work.


Police estimated the crowd to number
1880, while other sources placed the
total much higher.


Police did not know who did the
shooting. An officer who was riding
in the cab of the truck said he fired two
shots into the ground and two into the
air, but that the death-dealing bullets
were fired later. Witnesses said the
latter shots came from the truck after
1t rolled over.


WalkOut Closes Other Mills.


Virtually every other hosiery mill in
Philadelphia has been closed by the
walkout, and strikers from all parts of
the city congregated at the Cambria
plant. Fifty police were already on
guard because of previous disorders in
the eight-week strike, but they were
overwhelmed when the trouble started.


Eight automobiles carrying workers
had broken through the picket lines,
although every window was broken by
missiles, when the truck appeared. In
1t were IA employees.


The crowd rushed the truck and
bowled it over, trapping the workers
inside. Then the pickets began batter
ing at the vehicle and the shots rang
forth.


Norwood was killed instantly and
Minor died soon afterward in q hos
pital. William Madison, who was among
the demonstrators. was struck on the
shin by a glancing bullet.


Police Charge Crowd.


Police charged the crowd and took
the workers inside of the plant, later
removing them to a police station for
questioning.


Windows in the plant-particularly
one displaying an N. r. A. banner, were
the targets for bricks and stones. The
barrage was answered with lead weights
hurled by persons inside the building.


Among those hurt were two police
men. The officer riding on the truck
was struck in the face by brick, and
another officer was hit on the head
with lead weight. The latter is in a
serious condition.


Fire also came into the industrial
strife for the first time today. The
garage OF Whinneys Express Co., in
Northeast Philadelphia, closed by q
strike of drivers and helpers, was ignited
with oil-soaked rags despite a 24-hour
police guard. The blaze was quickly
extingulshed


Two girl pickets were arrested outside
midcity pocketbook establishments on
charges of attacking other girls who
were reporting for work They were
later discharged with warnings by a
magistrate.

In a fourth drastic relaxation

Direct purchases were author
lied from winners. Federal in

effective period of permits to
distribute were tripled.

agencies to the States and cities.

tically reduced it's forces. In the
third place Congress so liberalized

liquor that physicians may pre-
scribe virtually any reasonable
amount for the use of their
patients.

instead of one gallon of sacra-
mental wine for a years use,

raised from to 10 gallons.

charged with the responsibility

tions, although they must keep a
record stewing the name and

LEBANON TOWNSHIPS, N. j., May

climbed out Of the car.

NEW YORK, January 21.-An influx
Of buyers to national conventions Of
trade organizations broadened purchases
in the wholesale markets here this
week, but the mild weather slowed the
demand for heavyweight clothing and
other seasonable goods, retail stores
report.


Recent reductions in coffee and soap,
along with increased sales stats on
the road and wider advertising. have
helped swell sales Of grocery jobbers
in such lines as beverages, packaged
cereals, -four, sugar, starch, syrups.
canned vegetables and fruits.


Reports from road salesmen have
heartened makers Of mems and boys
clothing. Consuming centers continue
to call for small shipments Of raw
cotton, yet the cheapness Of that COM
modify makes it possible to offer per-
Gales and other types Of cotton dresses
at record low prices, with the result
that such merchandise Is moving.


As long as general industrial opera
tions remain limited, coal demand will
be light, but 1t showed some better
ment this week. Crude oil and gaso-
line stocks increased, resulting in
further price reductions. Plate and
window glass sales are rather slow,
but the automotive trade has enlarged
its takings Of safety glass.

12-year old Dorothy Gates. 24l0 Twen-

tearfully that she had been getting bad

unhappy since coming to Washington

slipping as they grasped the ledge when

drop, but changed her mind on find
ing she could not regain the sidewalk
unassisted.


Dorothy, police said. promised never
to try such thing again. The bridge
was almost deserted when the Incl
dent occurred. shortly after 9 pm.

NEW YORK, November 1.-Theres

Boy that has learned bitter lesson
never poke your beak at q clam.


This gull spied the clam-a big
fellow-lying just under the water yes
terday with his mouth open. The bird
stuck its nose into the clam. which was
disastrous, for the latter snapped its
jaws shut.


Then began q battle and much
churning of water as the bird tried to
free itself. The clam held on and
pulled the gull beneath the surface.

Kelly ran up, pulled of his shoes and
waded out to where the struggle was
going on.


He reached into the water and
brought out a clam as big as his two
fists with the sea gull still hanging on.
The policeman tried to pry open the
steel-jawed clam with a pocketknife,
but was unsuccessful.


Then he drew his club and whacked.
That did the business. The CLAIMS
shell broke and the gull was freed
with just pep enough to fly away.

Associated Press Financial Writer.


NEW YORK, July 29.-With trading
hours curtailed and extreme huctua-
tions of grains limited, financial mar
kets were able to cool down this week
and recuperate from the recent cor
rective" movement.


Wall Streets second thoughts on the
smashing decline of the previous week
bore out its earlier conclusion that the
tanning Of speculative spirits had been
timely and beneficial. especially since
there was no evidence that the break
had been more than a delayed technical
checking Of prices.


Quotations in major markets tended
higher through most Of the trading
period Stocks. as measured by the
Standard Statistics-Asosciated Press
averages, rebounded from 76.6 on Fri
day, July 81, to 84.8 on Thursday, July
81, sliding back a little yesterday when
the market closed for the week. The
extreme recovery was about 40 per cent
of the break from the years peak
reached July Is, and represented
natural rebound.


Wall Street took things easy on Fri
day, wondering meanwhile as to when
the widely expected secondary reac-
ton" from the recovery would appear
Most brokerage houses felt that such a
movement was probable and traders be-
gan to take sideline positions pending
developments. Pool interests were quiet.


The week brought striking evidence
of second quarter accomplishments by
business. United States and Bethle-
hem Steel Corporations reported a bal
ance of income from operations, both
making public the best statement since
1881, General Motors had a very
profitable three months. It's earnings
OF 80 cents common share were about
eight times those Of the same quar-
ter last year.

HARIS, February Apparently
- spurred by the possibility that


the Davis Cup may be wrested


from France, where it has been
held for six years, the record d-equaling
total of 80 nations have entered for the
1888 international tennis classic.


The entry list u three greater than
In 1881 and 1882 and is equaled only by
that of the boom year Of 1928. South
Africa, Peru and Argentina are the
three new challensers.


The United States heads the four ma

zone. Five are entered in the South
American zone and "a in the European
zone


The entries by zones:


North American-United States, Can
ada, Cuba, Mexico.


South American-Argentina, Brazil,
Chile, Peru and Uruguay.


European-Australia, Austria, Bel
giusn, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Eng
land, Egypt. Finland. Germany, Greece,
Holland, Hungary, Ireland. India, Italy,
Japan. Jugoslavia, Monaco, Norway,
Poland. Rumania, South Africa. Spain
and Switzerland.


THE record entry for the Davis Cup
i in q year that has witnessed so


much retrenchment in sport testi-
fies to the strong appeal that this in
ternational tennis competition exerts
throughout the world.


The growth Of the Davis Cup matches
in scope has been remarkable. Start
ing In 1900 as dual match between
the British Isles and the United States
for the trophy put up by Dwight F.
Davis. the competition spread to France
and Belgium in 1904 and Australasia
and Austria came In the following year


Canada, South Africa and Germany
entered the lists next, but it was not
until after the World War that the
Davis Cup became worldwide in its
appeal to rival the Olympics in its
international scope.


During the past decade the number
OF competing nations has jumped from
not more than a dozen to almost three
times that many.


OUNCE 1927 the Davis Cup has been
- held by France. That year Rene


Lacoste, Henri Cochet, Jean Borot-
"a and Jacques Brugnon defeated
Americas veterans, William Tilden and
William Johnston, at the Germantown
Cricket Club and won the cup for
France for the first time.


England. Australia and the United
States have been the only other ma
tions to capture the trophy, the United
States holding 1t from 1920 through
1926.


The United States is favored to bring
back the cup this year With Ellsworth
Vines ranked as the worlds leading
player on the strength of his two vic
tories over Cochet last year, Americas
young stars are expected to end Frances
long sway, although Tilden recently
picked the defending nation to win
again.


Germany, Australia. England and
Japan will also have to be reckoned
with seriously this year Germany sue
ceeded England as the strongest team
In the European zone last year.

HAVANA, Cuba. April 14.-Troops
were called to stamp out terrorism today
after II bombs explosions killed one
person and injured three or four.


The blasts came yesterday and last
night on the heels of several anony-
nous letters to police headquarters
warning that yesterday would start
RED week in Havana"


Cavalry was called out after police
had started roundup of persons sus-
pected of terroristic tendencies and op-
position to the rule of President Ma
chado. The mounted troops patroled
Galiano street, while throughout the
city automobiles were stopped at gun
point and searched.


Score Under Arrest.


Police seized a score of youths, in
cluding three unidentified students who
were taken from the fifth police sta
tion to Atares Castle. Police patrols
armed with machine guns guarded
against further outbreaks.


One bomb exploded not far from the
new home of Orestes Ferrara, former
Ambassador to the United States and
now secretary Of state in the Machado
government.


1t was hidden in a fruit vendors
wagon and 1t killed 3-year-olu Jose
Montana. Three men were reported
seriously injured in this and other
blasts.


Shooting started when police said
they found Manuel Garcia, 10, placing
bomb at street corner. Garcia was
probably fatally wounded. The bompings
were attributed by police to political
terrorism and SO quickly did they follow
one another that police and newspaper
men could hardly keep up with them.


Explodes Near Palace.


One bomb did slight damage at the
Church of the Angel, which is near the
Presidential Palace. Father Francisco
Abascal, inside the church, suffered
nervous shock.


Windows were shattered near q jewelry
and photographers shop. A school
building was damaged slightly.


Rifles were issued to the police. Mill
tary censors ordered nothing be pub
lished concerning the bombings.

was cited for bravery by both the

industry itself to cause pessimism. On

BY the Associated Press.


NEUNKIRCHEN, Saar Territory,
Germany, February 11.-From the
wreckage left by yesterdays terrific ex-
plosion of gas storage tank near
the Neunkirchen Iron Works 68 bodies
were taken today, but it was feared
that 200 more were buried under the
ruins of the big machine shop. which
could not be reached for the moment
because of the piles of debris.


Rescue workers dug increasingly
through the piles of glass, brick and
timber, ignoring the threat of tottering
walls. Doctors and nurses did what
they could for the injured. and every
where the relatives Of men still missing
poked about in the ruins. -------


More than 800 were in the hospitals
with serious injuries and 1900 or more
were slightly hurt.


Many persons were trapped and
killed in crowded street car which
was passing the big iron works at the
moment Of the blast. Then fire broke
out which spread destruction. This was
brought under control early today.


WnOkc tauey Sndkeu.


The blast was felt throughout the en-
tire upper Rhine Valley from Cologne
to the Swiss border. In many Rhine
land cities the people believed an earth
quake had shaken the district.


Hardly pane Of glass remained in
tact in an area 10 miles in diameter
surrounding the iron works. Three or
four smaller blasts followed the first
one.


Many women and children were
among the injured and every hospital
in the city and nearby area was filled
to capacity. Comparatively few men
were at work at the time of the blast
because of renovations being made in
the iron works. In the surrounding
area the streets were filled with the
debris Of homes and shops.


Three Killed in Theater.


New shifts were coming to work and
others were leaving. The streets were
crowded with these men, many of whom
were injured Three persons were
killed when ceiling fell in a movie
theater.


The force of the explosion hurled
bodies across streets. All telephone
lines in the vicinity were broken and
LrdlIlS were unable 10 eIltcr Lue railroad
station until early today because Of
wreckage on the tracks.


The tank which exploded was 270
feet high and $50 feet in diameter.


Neunkirchen has a population of
1000.


Trucks Become Ambulances.


More than 500 rescue workers were
on the job early today. All available
Eto oy~vr1
houses were converted into hospitals as
the number OF injured was increasing
and many more were expected to die.


The cause of the explosion and the
amount of damage was not Immediately
determined.


The Saar Government Commission
was summoned to discuss immediate re-
lief measures. The German Reich was
being approached for financial aid, for
the majority here are its nationals.


The catastrophe was the most serious
in this region since 1921, when SOS were
killed by an explosion at the Oppau
ammonia factory.

without ceremony, DR.. Fabio Lozano,

force two years from the time OF rat
ification.

lombian products will be admitted to

duties, excise taxes, and certain restric-

exempt from State excise taxes affect
ing Interstate commerce, where those
come under the jurisdiction of the Fed
eral Government.


The Colombian products involved
were not made public, but it Is known
that coffee is the principal product.

HALIFAX, Nova Scotia, July

coffin, Mrs. Richard Luddington
and her four small children, who
were burned to death in their
home, will be buried today in the

where they met their tragic fate.

the children, had the heartbreak-
ing experience of seeing his whole
family wiped out as their dwell
ing went up in smoke yesterday.

early and lit a lamp. The lamp
exploded and flaming oil was
scattered in all directions.


Aflame from head to feet, he
rushed outside in panic. He was
severely burned. His wife and
the four children were trapped
in their beds.

line for paraffin before retiring

the Court of the Belvedere. Ever
since the year 1927 they have
taken the oath on this day, which

supplied the papal guards. The
entire corps were present at the
taking of the oath and in addi-
tion 800 Swiss pilgrims looked on.


The officers wore the red vel
vet of great occasions and the men
had their halberds, their red, yel-
low and black costumes and their
plumed helmets, besides their
shining breast plates underneath
which was their old-world mailed
shirt Of iron, which no army in
Europe wears nowadays but which
has been preserved for it's pic
turesque effect among the Swiss
Guards.

northwestward. uprooting trees

Yeaton picked up a disabled yacht
with 13 aboard off Egmont Key,
FLA, and later put in at Tampa.
The patrol boat Corwin picked
up an oil barge with seven aboard
which had been adrift off the
Louisiana coast since Saturday
night.

4 FTER he graduated to the middle

Loughran showed his best form

but was ordered to fight Jimmy Slat-
terry. His victory over the Buffalo
fash clinched the title.


Loughrans first defense of his newly
Won honors was against Leo Lomskl.
In this fight Tommy rose to what
appears to be the highest point reached
in his long career. LonSki tore out
soon after the bell sounded and dropped
Tommy with right to the jaw. Dazed
and tottering around on rubbery legs,
the Philadelphian was battered all over
the ring fully two minutes before an
other crushing right sent him down for
another nine count. Loughran man
aged to get up and last out the round.
Boxing instinct alone saved him, as he
fenced superblv until his head cleared
during the next four rounds. From
then on he sliced and cuffed Lomski
every time the latter attempted to score
with wild swings and finished up with
an amazing burst of speed that earned
him the decision.


Loughran defended his title two more
times before he challenged Sharkey for
the American heavyweight crown
Mickey Walker and James J. Braddock
were his opponents. Again his superior
defensive and boxing tactics saved him.
Walker ripped and slashed at Tommy
for 10 rounds. but could not penetrate
beyond the champions long left jabs.
Braddock was no match for the skillful
Philadelphian.


Loughran has had his innings. He
has been able to go along during the
past two years against a poor lot of
heavies with titular pretensions. Box
ing seems to be lost art among the
big fellows. Too much reliance has
been placed on the wallop, so the clever
Loughran has been able to outscore the
crude though willing fighters.

running board Of the robbers car.

lege, directed at the tires of the car.

the bank escaped as the flight began.
Five others we're freed in the excite
ment attending a collision of the bandit
machine and another near the edge OF
the city.


Communicating a passing car. the
robbers fled with Miss Hilaria Schmidt,
%, bank bookkeeper, as their prisoner.
Four miles out of town, Alex Weltz, city
marshal, drew near in another machine
which halted when the robbers opened
fire. Weltz lodged behind his car only
to be run over when the excited driver
backed up inadvertently.


Take More Captives.


The robbers added three more host
eges, Mr.. and Mrs. Ed Wagner and
their baby, at farm near Vincent
Kans., where they changed to Wagners
truck.


The hostage list grew when passing
motorist was halted, his car tested but
found unsuitable, and he was placed on
the truck.


Near Holyrood. Kans., hostages and
truck we're left behind after the rob-
bers stole a new car, owned by an oil

ANNAPOLIS, Feb. 15.-A man
believed to be Howard F.. Stone
sifer, %. former watchman at
the Naval Academy. was burned
to death in a fire that destroyed
his home early today after a
party at which there was con-
siderable drinking, police said.


Further investigation into the
case was ordered by authorities
when neighbors reported that
they heard three shots fired dur
ing the party.


Buckle and Keys


Doctors were ordered to
examine the charred body to de-
termine if the man had been
shot.


Identification of the body was
based on the fact that a oelt
buckle with the initial IS" and
the key to StoneSifer's automobile
were found beside the body,
which was burned beyond recogni-
ton, and the fact that the man
has not been seen since the fire
started.


According to Acting Coroner
Thomas G. Basil, the six persons
attending the party were Stone
Sifer, who was reported as Sepa-
rated from his wife; Howard
Civens and Irving Ford. taxicab
drivers; and three girls, Rose
WEIGH, Leona Swink. and Edith
Brandenburg.


All Were Drinking


According to their story, Basil
said, there was considerable
drinking during the party, and
the five left about 2 o'clock in
the morning.


They denied that there was any
trouble or that any shots were
fired while they were in the
house, Basil said.


Neighbors gave different story
to police, however, saying that
there was considerable noise in
the house until about 4 o'clock in
the morning.


MIS-. bland spencer, a nelgnDOT,
reported that she heard the three
shots efired at about that time,
and shortly afterward she smelled
smoke, got up to investigate, and
found the house in flames.


Worked at Academy


The fire department was called.
but arrived too late to save the
six-room frame structure, which
was located at Lucas Avenue in
West Annapolis. The house had
been rented by Stonesifer from
DR.. Charles N. Taylor, of An
napolis.


Police said they would again
question those attending the party
today, and if it should be proved
that Stonesifer was shot, would
place the matter in the hands of
the grand jury.


The dead man was discharged
from the Naval Academy about
two weeks ago, it was said.

ruling that Annapolis could not
hold an election in 1888, to be
void, the Court of Appeals yes
terday gave the local politicians

fore the election could not be
held under the new provisions.
This was handed down in a per
curiam opinion and it was felt
that it barred the city from vot-
ing.


The opinion yesterday was an
enlargement of the original one
and by declaring the entire act
invalid the court gave the city
the right to hold its election
under the old law.


Mayor Walter E. Quenstedt,
Republican, present incumbent,
will compete with Charles Chance
local ship builder and a Demo
crat for the mayoralty.

BY the Associated Press.


The fate Of the boldest American
bid for commercial supremacy In the
air hung in the balance today as the
Nation took stock of the disaster that
befell the sky queen Akron.


For just Is months, the giant craft
was supreme as the largest, finest and
most complete ship Of its kind ever
built She represented the last word
both In German Zeppelin building skill
and adaptation of Yankee inventive
genius to the science Of aviation.


Macon Awaits Trial.


Even as she fell to her tragic end
however, her sister ship. the Macon
marking dirigible construction refine
ments born of the building and oper-
ating experiences with the Akron
awaited in her hangar the word that
would launch her upon an initial trial
voyage.


While these two ships were built and
carried on Navy basis as combat
craft, major purpose behind con-
struction was exploration of the trans
oceanic commercial possibilities of these
mighty liners of the air.


Such pioneering work underlay the
purely naval purposes for which they
were authorized. The Akron and the
Macon were free from the international
agreement that made the German
Zeppelin built Los Angeles only a com
mercial vessel. Thus they have afforded
opportunity also for Navy tests Of the
military usefulness Of such ships as
long range scouting craft and bombers


Held Most Airworthy.


The Akron had been considered by
experts the most airworthy and safe
airship in the world. Charges ranging
from sabotage to faulty construction
had been Investigated by congressional
committee and declared groundless.


The loss Of the Shenandoah in 1925
had prompted the Navy to increase
markedly the strength requirements for
airship design, and soon the Akron was
In the air again.


A vital factor was that the United
States, alone Of all the nations building
such aircraft, had helium gas with
which to I'LL the great ships cells, thus
drastically reducing the danger Of fire
which had destroyed many dirigibles IN
other countries.


The Akron completed her trial flight
September %, 1881. with marked success
and had since ridden out several severe
storms with only minor damage.

The four defendants in the Ecklund
murder trial were found guilty of Sec

2:45 O'Clock by jury in the District
Supreme Court.

from 20 years to life.

colored, and Albert Ernest Cash, 20,

pay roll robbery near the new House
Office Building January 20.


The verdict came exactly "a hours
after the case was given to the jury.
The jurors were locked up overnight
and have been in the jury room since
9 o'clock this morning with a short
respite for lunch.


None Of the defendants, with the
exception of Blackwell, showed any sign
of emotion at the verdict. Blackwell
smiled broadly, as If pleased.


The Government had asked the death
penalty for the four men and the trial
had been fought throughout only to
enable them to escape the electric
chair.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala, April 28.-The
nine colored men involved in the Scots
boro case were on a bread and water
diet today. after a Jail mutiny.


They rebelled in the day room" yes
terday, where they had been taken for
exercise, threatened their guards with
clubs improvised from water pipes and
light fixtures, and refused to return to
their quarters. They said their rebellion
was against mistrea tment.


Warden F. L. Erwin announced the

tacklng two white women in a case
which has attracted international atten-
ton.


AS the warden approached. he said
the nine prisoners refused to 90 back to
their cells. defied jail officials, and sent
out cardboard on which was printed
Freedom for the Scottsboro boys" and
demands for better treatment"


Sheriff Hawkins joined the warden
and other Jail attaches, but although
two or three Of the prisoners agreed to
lay down their weapons others shouted
We'll die flrst!" And one cried out
We will see the United States Supreme
Court and settle everything"


Sheriff Hawkins and Warden Erwin
finally left the nine locked in the day
room and the bread and water punish
ment was ordered


Warden Erwin said Haywood Patter-
son, 19, recently convicted a second
time in the case and re-sentenced to
death, was the leader of the rebellion
The mutiny. me said, apparently was due
to resentment over their being locked
IL separate room on visitors day.
This. he explained. was necessary be-
cause they had so many callers the Jail
corridors were jammed

MOSCOW.-RusSia is now emerging

a famine as the one which devastated

war.


The more recent famine was not due
to the shortage of crops. 1t was man

was the inexorable result of the eco
nomic dislocation which came two years

Union decided to bring the peasants

Many peasants in 1881 resented the

peasants. The Winter of 1882 and '33

shortage of work, animals and short

try.


Famine Allowed to Come.


From the viewpoint of the leaders of
the Soviet Union their policy of alloca-
ton was wise. They pursued it per-

premise on the whole mercifully. Their

policy millions of Russian peasants have
died from what are known as hunger
diseases: Typhus, tuberculosis and
dysentery. The number is placed

ably from 100000 to 100000 peasants

While Chinese leaders protested

Apparently executing the spirit

chukuo and Japan, the troops
advanced, along the military road
between Kuyuan and Dolonor.
the old Inner Mongolia capital.


Dolonor is only twelve miles
from Shangtu, ancient capital
of the Kublai Khan, great Mon
gol leader who in the thirteenth
century conquered all of China
and established Buddhism as the
state religion.


Despite bitter cold, the Japanese
proceeded with the construction of
an air base at Kuyuan. only so
miles north of the strategic Peip-
ing-Suiyuan railway. This air
base has caused grave concern
among Chinese leaders.

ST. JOHNS Newfoundland, March

Residents of Horse Island. two miles
east of Western Island, said they saw
a fire on the latter island yesterday
and today and believed that the seal
hunters had reached shore there. The
men carried food sufficient for three
days.


1t was believed that when the weather
becomes milder they can make their
way to the mainland. 20 miles south.
Western Island is large, and although
uninhabited, affords shelter.


The sealers could not communicate
with Horse Island or the mainland
Six steamers now are in the northern
ice fields in search of seals, but 1t Is
thought they will net attempt to force
their way into White Bay unless ab-
solutely necessary.

LANSING, Mich, Feb. II GIN.
S.).-The Michigan legislature to-
day took the first step toward es-
tablishing an emergency dictator
ship to cope with the situation
created by the States eight-day
banking moratorium.


The senate unanimously passed
a resolution declaring state OF
emergency and requesting the
governor to assume almost abso-
lutte power over the banks.


The resolution was sent imme-
diately to the House, but due
to the fact that many Represent
atives were away from the Cali
tai attending Democratic county
conventions, action was post
poned until Monday.


The resolution embodied the ef-
fects of all the emergency bills
now pending before the legisla-
ture, permitting the governor to
control the banks after the eight
day "holiday'' ends February %.
The holiday was declared to save
Detroit's Union Guardian Trust
Company, which threatened to
collapse and shatter the States
financial structure.


Under the resolution, the gov
ernor will in effect make his own
laws until the legislature can have
time to pass emergency measures
which will stand the test of the
courts.

haikwan to Kopeiko. remains in the
hands of the Japanese. who do not in

LANSING, Kans.. May 30.-Eight

game.

the men fled through the main gate
with Prather

the convicts. He was shot in the right
arm.

an automobile and drove away.

Kansas City, about Is miles distant.


Authorities in surrounding cities were
notified and sent squads of police and
deputy sherifTs to guard highways.


Other reports said that three guards
had been kidnapped. Their names were
given as Laws, Lindsey and Powell.

BOSTON. August 14.-Several pris-
oners were believed to have escaped
during riotous outbreak in the House
of Correction on Derr Island just be-
fore the noon hour today.


A half hour later prison officials re-
ported two had been returned and they
were checking to determine how many
had made good their break. They be-
lieved the number did not exceed three
inmates.


The uproar began. officials said, just
before the lunch period. About score
of inmates made a break for liberty
during the trouble. Several, estimated
at four or five, seized a truck and drove
across Shirley Gut, a narrow, shallow
channel which separates the island
from the mainland.


Guards Return Two.


Later guards returned to the island
with the truck and two Of the escaped
inmates. Other guards meanwhile sue
ceeded in quieting the other prisoners


The entire jail population of LAS
gathered in the dining hall for lunch
participated in the riot which preceded
the dash for liberty Suddenly one of
the inmates beat his tray with a cup
apparently a arranged signal, and
the dining hall was thrown into an
uproar. TableS were overturned and
dishes buried. Guards fired shots in
the air in an unsuccessful attempt tC
reStore order. While the riot was at
its height, five men leaped out a WIN
dow and jumped into an auto truck
Shortly after they drove across Shirley
Gut the truck was brought back In
it was one Of the prisoners, bloody and
unconscious.


Blame Concord Gang.


Prison officials blamed the outbreak
on the so-called "Concorn gang,
known bad actors" who had been
transferred to the island from the
Concord Reformatory.


"Yammering" continued in the din
ing hall until the inmates we're returned
to their cells.


Riot calls to the Winthrop and Bos-
ton police brought large details armed
with riot guns to the scene Winthrop
police patrolled the beach on the main
land and reported they saw several men
swimming in the water. Whether those
men were among the five who fled in
the truck, at least three of whom were
subsequently, captured, could not be de-
termined Immediately.

Memory and Faith are both
invisible reachings. There are
certain definite steps toward re-
membering. You don't realize
you use them; but wise men,
who. study the mind, have map
ped them out. When you want
to remember something, this is
what you do.


Some need in you urges you
to remember something.


Instantly your mind turns
back toward remembering that
one certain thing. It begins
searching-begins rejecting all
other memories-goes on dog
gedly looking, looking, certain
that the thing it wants is
there. Suddenly-perhaps in a
split second, perhaps after long
hours-your mind presents you
with the picture or the fact
you want.


That's how memory works.
And faith works in much the
same way. Faith isn't an aim
less, emotional hocus pocus. It,
too, has definite steps which
you must observe.


FIRST-You must decide
what you want to get, just as
you decided what you wanted
to remember.


SECOND You must feel
that it's practical and possible
to get that thing; that it is
within the range of your per-
sonal handling. There's no
sense in making a lot of cock
eyed demands, and then beef
ing because you can't get
them. There, are certain things
which belong in your life
certain things you can handle,
and other certain things which
you can't. Decide that the
thing you want is possible for
you and right for you.


THIRD-Having decided this,
put all other desires and doubts
out of your head. Go after that
thing you want. as your mind
went after that memory. Go
after it doggedly, unfalteringly.
Use all ipgenuity-every prac-
tical help within your power.
But don't depend on those out
ward gestures to do the trick.
The real power lies in your own
mental aim. Keep that aim
unfaltering. Don't let your
self be diverted. Don't waste
your energy in thinking over
past failures. Cleave through
your confusions as your mind
Glove through the chaos Of
memories.


THE THING YOU NEED
THE THING YOU HAVE A
RIGHT TO-IS WAITING FOR
YOU. GO GET IT!


And you CAN get it!


With what?

NEW YORK, November 16.-Trading
was quiet and price changes mixed on
the Curb Exchange today. Fluctuations
in the more active stocks were small
either way.


The market was slightly higher at
the opening, but turned irregular owing
to a lack of buying orders rather than
to pressure of offerings. Traders were
disinclined to hold commitments over
the week end in view of the confused
monetary situation.


The oils, the strongest group In the
market all week, were subjected to
some profit-taking today and activity
in them subsided temporarily. Stand
ard Oil of Indiana was in supply, as
we're Standard Of Kentucky and South
Penn Oil. international Petroleum,
Imperial OIL and Humble OIL. which
early in the week reached new high
levels for the year, held better than the
others. Gulf OIL Of Pennsylvania was
quiet and a shade easier.


The Canadian gold mining stocks,
which broke sharply in Fridays session,
showed mixed tendencies today. Lake
Shore Mines was still under pressure,
but Wright-Hargreaves Mining, Hol-
linger Gold and Hudson Bay Mining
were firm. Newmont Mining was steady.
In the silver group, Bunker Hill-Sulli-
van Mining and Gorham Manufactur-
ing eased.


Electric Bond g. Share braced after
its declines of the last few sessions, but
the utilities generally had a heavy ap-
pearance. American Gas & Electric
common and preferred were soft. Co.
lumbia Gas & Electric convertible pre-
ferred. which dropped 4 points Friday,
slipped more today. Alabama Power
81 preferred eased.

stock and the announcement that the
companys new American subsidiary
would involve an investment Of $4,000
900. Distillers. Ltd. and Distillers- Sea
grams scored modest gains


The close was quiet and irregular
The oils became increasingly active
toward the finish, with Humble Oil
squirting points.

LONG BEACH, Cal, July S
GN.SO.-With their limbering-up
exercises finished, the Eastern in
vaders, Yale, Harvard and Cornell,
were ready to participate in time
trials today on the Olympic
course in preparation for the ma
tional intercollegiate regatta Fri
day and Saturday.


The three western crews, Cali.
fornia, Washington and Univer-
sity of California at Los Angeles,
also planned to hold time trials
today, with the result that the
placid waters Of the Marine sta
dium will be churned to tidal
wave proportions during the day.


Yale Is Co-Favorite


In their early workouts this
week, Harvard and Cornell showed
surprising strength, and their
blade-work was even smoother
than that Of the Yale crew, which
ranks as a co-favorite with Wash
ington.


Most of the time until today
has been spent in short Sprints
and fast starts, and-in this con-
nection-the Harvard boys have
been particularly smooth. Whether
they have enough power to cope
with Yale, however, was to be
proved today when the crews line
up against the watch.


The revamped Cornell crew
has shown satisfactorily, and
Coach Jim Wray is determined to
leave the boating alone: while
Charles Whiteside, Harvard men
tor, also was through experiment.
ing with his lineup.

Yale, with its same sprint crew
which Coach Ed Leader compares
favorably with the Olympic cham
pions of '24, kept it's lineup in
tact. Leaders only job was to
bring these boys from the four
mile grind to the short sprint
and today's test should prove how
well he has succeeded.


With Edward Argensinger,
Washington stroke, suffering from
an injured back, Coach AL Ul-
Erickson anticipated today's work.
out with keen interest. While
he has made no move to sub
stitute for Argensinger, Ulbrick-
son reserved his decision until

BY the Associated Press.


Soviet Russia's new order that all
Russians must have passports and pol
Icy Of careful checking by the police
SO that only those who work viii eat is
part of movement to stamp out the
spirit of wanderlust which has hindered
railway traffic since the initiation of
the bolsheviSt regime.


Russian trains, freight and passenger
trains alike, have been crowded with
wanderers ever since the Cars armies
began to disintegrate The roofs and
platforms of many passenger trains
have been filled with men, women and
children floating aimlessly from place
to place.


Drifting Becomes Habit.


In the early days of the Soviet regime
many of the informal travellers really
were ex-sold--r3 seeking their homes
and relatives. They feigned comrade-
ship with the trainmen and travelled
in such large numbers that railway off,
cials could not have hindered their
movements.


In the famine years of 1921 and 1922
there was flight from the parched
wheat areas that officials made little
effort to check.


But travel became a habit with a
great army Of hoodlums and ne'er-do-
wells who have drifted from place to
place during the four years the new in
dustrial plan has been operating and
have worked only long enough in any
one place to get clothing and money
to carry them on their pilgrimage.


Complain Of Turnover.


Foreign engineers in charge Of con-
struction Of new industries have re-
peatedly said the tremendous turnover
in labor was their chief handicap
Workmen, in turn, frequently have
charged that insufficient food and sup
plies make 1t necessary for them to
move on in search of better living


In recent years the tremendous growth
Of Moscow taxed housing facilities and
made the capital a refuge for non
workers who live by their wits and are
able to get food cards even If they are
not workers.


Coincidentally with the passport order
the Soviet regime has also announced
that women of working age who are
not gainfully employed shall be denied
food privileges, but may buy food in
the open markets, where prices are pro-
hibitive. This order affects home
makers.

NEW YORK, December 11.-Col.

ana Texas Ranger, died yesterday of
heart disease in his hotel suite here.
He was &c and had been i'll several

Born in Texas. Col. Feigl began his
newspaper career as a reporter on the
Houston Post. Later he was connected
with the New York Record, the New
York Press, the Telegraph, and the
Herald before it was merged with the
Tribune


He and his brother, Capt. George
Feigl, who survives him, founded the
Iammany Times in 1893. The paper
later became the Political Review,


His military career was begun with
the Texas National Guard in the early
sos. With the rank of colonel. he
served on the stats of Cows. Ross, Hogg
and Culbertson of Texas. When Cara
was trying to overthrow the Diaz
regime in Mexico Col Feigl saw service
on the frontier with the Texas Rangers.

appointed chief of the Bureau of Spe-
cial Service of the New York Police
Department and organized the military
Intelligence division.

The Fort Sill, Okla, Field Artillery
School equestrian team won the annual
telegraphic horse show competition last

Kans.

Oy O1INO


Tonight's championship ring
battle between Primo Camera,
Italy's Man Mountain, and Jack
Sharkey, Boston's world cham
pion, brings to mind the fact that
the first international prize fight
of modern history also involved
an italian.


The scrap took place in Lon
don at the Figg's Amphitheater
in 1888, exactly two hundred years
ago, and the Italians opponent
was Bob Whitaker. an English
man. The London elite of the
day, both British and foreign.
were in attendance. The fight
is vividly described in Pierce
Egan's classical ring history
"Boxiana."


The Italians real name is un-
known, records listing him only
as the Venetian GondoNer. His
resemblance to the current AM
bling Alp is amazing. According
to writer's Of the day, the spec
tatorS gasped in wonder at his
prodigious size and build. He
lowered far above his none too
small rival. His arms were not
only big and powerful, but un-
commonly long. He was also par
ticularly fast for man of his
height and weight.
In fact, it is not improbable
that he was some ancient kin Of
the present pachyderm Of the
ring, for both hail from the same
region of italy, Venetia.


Jaw SmaSher


The giant italian came to Lon
don with reputation of having
smashed the jaws of the greater
number of those who dared to
oppose him in his homeland.


James Figg, first champion Of
England, who had retired in 1870,
promoted the match. Figg, be-
ing aware of the Italians jaw
breaking propensities, selected
Whitaker, noted for his granite
maxillary, in preference to the
two more fragile-jawed title claim
ants of the day, Tom Pipes and
Bill GREETING.


1t was fought with bare fists
under the London Prize Ring
Rules, with a knock-down termi-
mating the round, the fallen man
being allowed a half minute to
come to scratch for the next
round.


The original Ambling Alp
leaped across the ring, when time
was called and caught Whitaker
flush on the chin with a terrific
clout which knocked him out Of
the ring. The ring was built
much higher than those Of pres
ent days, and Whitaker hit the
hard ground with a hard jolt.
However, his seconds had him in
shape to resume the battle in
prescribed time. His quick re-
covery and the fact that his jaw
was still intact considerably sur
prised the invader, used to seeing
his foes stay down after such a
blow.


Realizes Handicap
Whitaker, realizing he could
not cope with the giant in the
accepted stand-up style, reSorted
to strategy. When the Venetian
again rushed him, the Britisher
lodged under his huge tree-like
arms and drove his fist into his
flabby stomach. The Gondolier
gasped with pain and astonish-
ment. This was something new
for him and decidedly unpleasant.
He had never been hit in the
bread-basket before.


Whitaker, sensing his advan-
tage, kept ducking under the
Venetian's sledge-hammer fists
and driving his own deep into
the ample target before him.
The Gondolier was soon writhing
on the floor.


His seconds managed to bring
him to scratch for the third
round, but Whitaker's persistent
pot-shots at his middle brought
him down again and this time
for keeps. Thus ended 1talyS
first bid for international boxing
recognition.


While Camera is the first full
blooded Italian to fight for the
world championship. Luis Angel
Firpo, who went down to defeat
in a hectic scrap with Jack
Dempsey, 10 years ago. though
born in Argentine, had an
Italian father.

DAYTONA BEACH, Fla, February
22.-Sir Malcolm Campbell, famous
British car driver, attained the aston
ishing speed Of 273 1856 miles an hour
on the first official run for new
world land speed record.


Despite the fact visibility was not
good Campbell was clocked over the
officially measured mile in 1915 Sec
onds.

the course, made from north to south,
Campbell stopped his car and gave it
a careful inspection before making
another run northward over the course.


Two runs, one in each direction are
necessary for him to establish a new
record and each must be made at an
average speed greater than his present
mark of 253 miles an hour.

ematical equations and charts,

HOLLYWOOD. May 31.-The film
| colony this week is knitting its col
| lective brow and wearing a studious air.
Before 1t has been placed a volumi-
nous document, the revised constitution
of the Academy Of Motion Picture Arts
and Sciences.


The institution with the imposing


name-the name was among the articles


not changed-will embrace more pow
ers when the document is ratified.
There will be meetings and discussions,


as usual, before this step is taken.
At its inception six years ago the
academy was rather formal, exclusive


group. It's Cancellation Committee has
functioned quietly In the settlement OF
! family squabbles" In the industry the
academy has succeeded in getting
courses in motion picture apprecia-
ton into several colleges; it has
! awarded, at an elaborate annual din


ner, trophies for outstanding work in
| various film fields, and 1t has fostered
research resulting in numerous tech


nical improvements.


Would Broaden Work.
Such activities would continue under
| the new constitution, some of them


broadened in scope. Essentially the
new deal" in academy affairs means
! that it will have changed from an aloof
! body to an organization functioning
actively for the advancement and pro-
lection of its members, and for the
amicable, self-government Of its COM
ponent branches.


The academy came actively to the
front in the recent salary-waiver crisis.
TtS Ernprpepcv Committee worked for
less stringent terms from the producing
companies. and won its points. It
fought not only for its members. but for
the majority on the outside. When the
smoke cleared away the move for re-
organization was on.


Under the new plan the academy


would be financially independent, sup
ported by membership dues, with con-
tributions from studios used only for
research. The employer group would be
admitted to corporate membership"
but producers Gas creative talenD would
form the fifth academy branch as at
present.


Everybody Must Behave.


All academy members would be
pledged to arbitrate their common diff
ficulties and to participate in establish
ment and enforcement of joint agree
ments. In other words. everybody must


behave and play fair or everybody else
will punish the offender.


The academy now has nearly 1000
members. with about 600 more actors,
writers, directors, technicians and pro-
ducers eligible, and the gates thrown
open. Henceforward, says the academy,
nom -joiners will have to fight their own
battles.

and the income Of factory workers had
regained quarter of the loss. while
the cost of living rose per cent from
March to September.


Meanwhile it was announced that

by the Labor Department showed an
increase Of nearly 2 per cent during
September bringing the increase over
a year ago to nearly 8l2 per cent.


The department said today the Bu-

1926 as 100 rose from 69.5 for August

Highest Since 1881,


The index for September averaged
above 70 for the first time since No
vember, 1881. and is higher than for
any month since october. 1881, when
the figure was 70.3. In September, 1882,

largely to increases in prices of cloth

which advanced rapidly for six months,

BY the Associated Press.


MADRID, June 8.-The government
headed by Premier Manuel Azana re-
signed today


The resignation came after a cabi-
net session and resulted directly from
the refusal of President Niceto Alcala
Zamora to make ministerial changes
requested by Premier kzana. The pre-
mier had asked that a new treasury
minister be appointed and that the
ministry Of agriculture be split into two
parts.


Confidence Lost.


When the President informed him he
would be unable to do this without con-
Sulting Republican minority leaders. the
premier declared Senor Alcala Zamora
no longer had confidence in the
cabinet.


Opposition to the Azana government,
which was formed December Is, 1881,
has been piling up for some time The
cabinets difficulties were increased ma
terially recently as result of con-
troversy over Spain's new religious laws


These laws, which were signed by
President Niceto Alcala Zamora last
week. turned religious orders into civic
groups and nationalized church prop
erty worth millions of dollars. Pope
Plus issued an encyclical declaring the
legislation constituted an attack not
only on the church, but on all religion,
and members of the Spanish govern
nent were automatically excommuni-
Gated.


Move Expected


The Radical Socialist bloc, headed by
former Foreign Minister Alexandra Ler-
roux, has been restive for some time
and political observers had expected 1t
to withdraw its support from the gov
ernment.


High government officials appealed
to the Radical Socialist convention yes
terday to continue their support, saying
that Spain was undergoing type Of
civil war between the parties of the
right and the left This civil war, gov
ernment spokesmen said, was exempli-
fed in the campaign against the
agrarian reform law and the religious
law.


The agrarian reform law provides for
the seizure of the estates of men who
were grandees under the monarchy. and
for the distribution Of this land among
the peasants.

With five of the men who helped

the Toronto Maple Leafs, cup holders,
in the fourth and decisive game Of the
championship series here last night,
10, in overtime.


Bill Cook, leading scorer Of the
National League, broke up the battle
after Z minutes "a seconds of overtime.
He grabbed pass from another Ranger
veteran, Butch Keeling, and beat Goalie
Lorne Chabot with ncat corner drive
from close in. Paving the way for
the winning goal were successive
penalties to Alex Levinsky and Bill
Thoms which left the Leafs two men
short and in no position to block the
Rangers last determined assault.


The victory was the Rangers third
in the -three-out-o -of-five series,
Toronto winning only one game. The
Rangers won the first game, ST., and
the second. 81, dropping the third
battle, 3-2.


TORONTO outplayed the Blue Shirts
i through the three regular periods,


but they could not break through
They peppered young Andy Aitkenhead
in the Ranger nets, with 48 drives in
that time, but the youngster blocked
them all.


AS the game went into overtime, the
Leafs suffered two bad breaks" and
the penalty box for a too-heavy body
check on Ossie Osmundson and Thoms
followed him moment later for hold
ing Art Somers in face-off.


The Rangers raced to the attack.
Out of one face-off, Keeling poked the
puck clear, raced over the Toronto Blue
line and passed to Bill Cook whose shot
beat Chabot cleanly.


The Rangers broke two records in
their march to the championship. Cecil
Dillon, young forward, accounted for
one of them when he scored eight goals
during the play-offs, one more than
Frank Boucher tailed in 1928 when he
set the modern" record. The Rangers,
as team, set new record by coming
from third place to win the cup. No
other team ever has accomplished that
feat. The Rangers first defeated the
Montreal Canadiens in the third-place
play-ons and then qualified for the
finals by eliminating the Detroit Red
Wings, survivors Of the second-p place
play-offs.

night, Bill and Bun Cook, Boucher,

HOLLYWOOD, CAL, July 3
G.NS0.-The love story Of
Doug" and Mary reads like a
Hollywood scenario-all save the
unhappy ending.


The romance began more than
13 years ago when Mary Pickford
was already established as the
"First Lady" of the screen and
Douglas Fairbanks was becoming
one Of the most popular heroes Of
the silent films. 80


The two were married on March
81, 1920. Soon they set about
building their 100000 home,
"Pickfair," as they plunged on
ward in their careers.


Then Came the Break


For 10 years they worked con-
stantly, amassing fortunes and
emerging as the unquestioned So
cial leaders of the movie set.


The talkies came, and other
stars Of silent films fell by the
wayside-but not so with Douglas
and Mary. The medium Of sound
only opened new fields to con-
Quer.


But three years ago Doug grew
tired of the klieg lights and
exacting routine Of the movie
studios.


There were vague reports that
the link that had bound them
together-common love Of the
films-had snapped. Hollywood
asked:


what has happened to
Mary. what has happened to
Doug?"


And the answer was that Doug
wanted to play golf and loaf
and that Mary wanted to go on
working.


England and Orient


Doug, it seemed, didn't care If
he ever made another picture.
Mary, superb actress and busi-
ness woman, could never desert
that Pickering celluloid that had
brought her fame and wealth and
position.


Even in 1880 there were rumors
Of divorce-promptly squelched by
intimates of the pair.


The occasion was their first
real separation in 10 years Of
ideal married life. Doug went to
England to see Bobby Jones win
another golf championship, and
Mary stayed home to work.


He telephoned her every day,
but the report that there was
trouble in "Pickfair" persisted.


"That's the annual 'lie,' and
here's our combined emphatic
annual denial" was the way
Doug dismissed the rumorS.


In 1881, Doug was shooting
tigers in the Orient and Mary
was alone in "Pickfair" on their
anniversary, and the report Of
separation flared anew.

BY the Associated Press.


ATLANTA, September 6.-Heavy rains
on the Georgia coast came from the
storm which today was reported by the
Weather Bureau between Savannah and
Macon.


The storm came into Georgia from
the West Indies, after passing through
parts of Florida. Its center moved very
slowly during the past "a hours. Light
rains extended into Alabama and Ten
nessee.


Rainfall was heaviest near the coast,
Savannah reporting $50 inches during
the past "a hours. Augusta had 1.26
inches, Macon 1872 and Thomasville
1.12.


Temperatures were moderately low in
Northern Georgia this morning.


The Weather Bureau expected the
storm to move up along the Atlantic
Coast more rapidly today.

marked the simple everyday life at

chusetts community.

mined the length of their visit, but be-
lieved they would stay the remainder
of the week.

with whom he was associated when
Gen. Dawes was member Of the Mill
tary Board of Allied Supply. Their
friendship brought the two men to-
gether frequently after Gen. Dawes be-
came Ambassador to Great Britain
Gen. Carter held the American Dis
tinguished Service Medal.

MINNEAPOLIS, May 80 LP).-Busi-
ness in the ninth Federal Reserve dis
trict was considerably better" in April
and early May than in earlier months
of 1888, the monthly review of the
district Reserve Bank here said yes
terday.


Higher prices for farm products and
reopening of banks provided basis for
improvement.


Country check clearings for the first
half of May indicate this months
spending of money will be the most
extensive since the Spring of 1881, the
review said.


THE improvement In country check
clearing has been especially pronounced
in the Dakotas and Montana. where
the effect of higher grain prices has
been direct" it commented.

I'VE beat ourselves" they

In other words, the Griffs are

narrows down to the happy
thought that the "boyS" are truly

ally defeated themselves out there

ticularly in the eighth inning

Thomas bad throw to first which

ondly, Thomas bad throw was

Fred Schulte's tumble in the sew.
enth was one, while Goose Cos.

error in the eighth, helped the

two days, according to meager
dispatches received here.

Islands, the hurricane was be.
lieved to have veered southwark
and to be spending its force over
a bleak and uninhabited area in
northern Mexico.


Citrus Crops Escape


The Texas border was ur-
affected by the storm, and the
rich Rio Grande Valley citrus
fruit and cotton area escaped
damage.


A 60-mile wind. however, con-
tinued to pound the Texas Coast
line early today.


Dispatches from fishing viii
lagos on the Mexican Coast re-
vealed the storm struck with a
terrible force, crumpling buildings
as though they were of sand, and
tossing fishing craft high on the
beach.


Coast Guardsmen stationed at
Padre Island, said the storm was
the worst they had experienced
since the station was established.

According to reports of meteor.
ologists in Southern Texas, the
hurricane swept inland between
the Rio Grande and Tampico,
about 35 miles south of the river,
and is now spending itself in the
desolate Mexican area just south
Of the Rio Grande.


Storm warnings, flying through
out this area for the past two
days, were ordered lowered today.

Deadly gas fumes spreading over

after noon.


First announcement stated that
a leak in an ammonia pipe was
the source of the gas, but after
a hasty investigation of the floor
ventilating system, it was indi-
Gated two tear gas bombs had
been thrown into an open pipe Of
the system.


The matter Immediately was
placed in the hands of the po-
lice.


More than 1000 persons were
routed from the exchange build
ing as all floors from the fifth
down were ordered closed.


Traders and exchange special
lists angrily, but willingly, left
their posts on the floor to flee
the acrid fumes. They choked
and their eyes burned from the
effects of the gas.

VIENNA, April 11.-Chancellor Engel-
bert Dollfuss' flying trip to Rome today,
where German Government leaders al
ready are visiting Vatican and Italian
government chiefs, was linked IN some
quarters with Premier MuSsolinis cam
ipaign for revision of postwar treaties.


1t brings together representatives OF
the three principal nations which have
been displeased with the frontier lines
set up after the World War. 1t also
brings together the leaders of three die
tatorial governments, Chancellor DOLL
fuss having ruled alone in Austria for
the last month.


Will See MussOlini.


An official announcement last night
said Dr. Dollfuss would visit Mussolini.
There were rumors that he would talk
with Capt. Hermann Goering, Naz1
member of the German cabinet. who IS
in Rome, concerning the establishment
of an auxiliary police force in Austria
similar to that instituted in Germany
under Capt. Goering's direction.


DR.. Dollfuss is going to Rome for the
same announced purpose that took the
other German leader, Vice Chancellor
Franz Won Papen to that city. They
both are Catholics and both ostensibly
bent on attending Holy week services in
Vatican City.


Ofsetting the possibility that the
Austrian chancellor will discuss the rpe-
cial police matter with Capt Goering
Is that there was no indication there
would be room for Austrian NaZis in the
force. The Heimwehr (Fascist) Organi-
zation was being prepared for the
auxiliary police.

movement for union of Austria and Ger
many and DR.. Dollfuss assumed dicta-
torial powers when the NaZis became
menacing Immediately after the Hitler
electoral victory in Germany. Both
Germany and Austria, however, regard

measure permitted them under military
restrictions set by the peace treaties.


Pension Cuts Announced.


The Dollfuss government has an
nounced drastic pension cuts. Instead
of war veterans, however, those imme-
diately affected are pensioned Federal
railway employees.

sioners and only 65 900 active employees,

saving.

Contracts with the Government must
be filed under their original terms, even
though the makers run into increased
operating costs due to application of the
national recovery act, Controller Gen
eral McCarl held today.


The decision was given to the Attor-
ney General, who had advised the con-
troller general that the Delta Finishing
Co. of Philadelphia had served notice
it could not complete a contract for
bleaching and shrinking duck manufac-
tured in Atlanta prison at the rate of
25s cents per yard, but would have to
boost the cost approximately 35 per cent
because the firm WAS operating under
the recovery code. The Attorney Gen.
eral asked what procedure should be
followed.


Cannot Modify Terms.


The controller general responded
that there is no existing legal authority
for modifying the contract, and added


THE contract between the United
States and the Delta Finishing Co.
constitutes an obligation binding on the
company and it may not withdraw
therefrom without resulting liability to
the United States for excess cost, If
any, which may be occasioned the
Government by such default"


In this instance, to fill out the con-
tract, will cost the Delta Co. about
$500 more than the original estimated
figure.


Legislation Likely.


The case is the first OF the sort to
arise and it was recalled today that at
the time the recovery act was under
discussion President Roosevelt said that
doubtless the next Congress would have
to enact legislation that would protect
contractors engaged on Government
work, on the basis of agreements which
would call for increased expenditures
under the act.

Lists Five Visitors.

cinct, nearby and notified police. II
took the officers who responded abou,
10 minutes to sever the bonds.


Police Immediately broadcast a look
out for the Stanleys, who are said tc
have lived here, conducting fortune
telling establishments on Seventh
street, before moving to Detroit. A de-
scription of their automobile was in
cluded in the lookout.


Mrs. Demetro was back in bed today
awaiting the return of her husband
Petro, from New York. Rosa, none the
worse for her experience, was doing the
family fortune telling.

NEW YORK. July 27.-More work.
ers with more money to spend are per-
suading ratail trade executives that the
bleak days are nearing happy end.


With unemployment abating and
mass consuming power widening lead
erS in the retail field look for sub
stantial increase in volume during the
latter half of 1888


Department store volume, for the
first six months of the year. averaged
some IS per cent under the correspond
ing period of 1882. However, the bulk
of this decline was a result of the
ravages of the first four months. May
and June operations made favorable
comparisons. June sales decreasing only
per cent from year ago.

kept pace with the recovery in indus
trial activity. However the enthusi-
astic response Of the country to the ad-
ministration's industrial recovery pro-
gram leads retail specialists to view this
condition as temporary.


A feature Of the trade in July has
been the continued expansion of sales
largely representing goods in the lower
price ranges-to industrial wage earn
els and generally throughout agricul-
tural districts.


In the grocery field sales of the out
standing distributors have been in
creased by rising prices. and in many
cases dollar sales are approaching last
years level. Actual sales volume has
likewise gained, but on more modest
scale.

Miss Jacobs victory"

Editor, McGill Commodity Service. Inc.


AUBURNDALE, Mass, April 8 (P).-
All commodities this week continued the
way since the bank moratorium In
early March. The increase was due
primarily to agricultural products,
which are discounting the inevitable
influence OF the farm relief bill. Out Of
IA individual groups. 8 advanced, 4 de-
clined, while one remained unchanged


Industrial Index Gains.


Industrial prices were higher due to
tighter quotations for the building ma
terial group, which featured an increase
In lumber quotations, q higher price
range for non-ferrous metals-the lead
ership taken by copper, tin and silver
Non-ferrouS metals were moderately
higher as the composite price of pig
iron was marked up. Paper and pulp
prices showed more disposition to re-
cover. Price strength has not been
accompanied by a corresponding i'm
provement in industrial activity. There
fore the upward trend is largely psy-
Geological rather than fundamental
The administration is gradually COM
pleting ways and means for higher
commodity price range.


Agricultural prices showed more
strength than any other group. Wheat
prices jumped to heights unreached in
over q year. On Thursday wheat was
up 7& cents, corn, 534 cents; oats, 8
cents and rye, 10 cents above the lows
Of the previous week. The upswing is
directly attributable to q combination
of unfayorable weather and the agita-
ton for possible legislative measures.


Live stock prices were moderately
buoyant, reaching a level 19 per cent
over the extreme low in this depression.


Building materials were higher, re-
fiecting the rebound in lumber. So
much low-grade lumber has been used
up during the past month in the manu-
facture of beer cases that this has af-
fected the grades utilized in construc-
tion. :.


Non-ferrous metals again showed
disposition to advance following the
reaction which took place in late March.
Even copper, under the handicap of
excessive reserve stocks, was marked up.


Ferrous metals are showing more re-
sistance to downward trend. The
composite price Of pig iron advanced
slightly.


Fine textiles were buoyant as wool
prices have been maintained and cot
ton has shown definite upward trend.
Silk also was moderately higher.


Important Price Changes.


The one group that remained steady
during the week was fuels. The four
groups that were slightly lower were
chemicals. hides and leather, paint
materials and vegetable oils.


Most important price changes in the
McGill Weekly Index.

tional Bank in Streator.


Braving a hail Of lead from

From sources close to the
Woodmont Country Club. it has
been learned that the club will
once again forego its annual in
vitation golf tournament.


Along with other local clubs,
Woodmont announced two years
ago the staggered system whereby
the invitation tournament would
be held alternate years. This
meant that the club would hold
no tournament in 1882, but would
return to the tournament calen-
dar in 1888, providing economic
conditions took the upswing.


Not Alone In Stand


The depression still hangs and
Woodmont deems it unwise to go
ahead with plans for a 1888 in
vitation event.


Nor is Woodmont alone in this
stand. There are several other
local golf clubs that will make
this so-called staggered tourna-
ment system look like Soviet Rus
sia's five-year plan.

shapes now, only Chevy Chase
and Army-Navy appear definitely
certain to hold events. There is
also a possibility that Manor

ton event two years ago, may
return to that particular field

applied for the sectional amateur
qualifying trials and have also
discussed a $4,000 open tourna.
ment for late spring or early
summer.

Past the Brazilian wilds the
route lay across mountain
range at the Venezuelan frontier

From here the trip was COM
paratively easy, being over Ven

then, finally, across the Gulf Of
Pa-ia, lying between Venezuela
and Trinidad, to Port-of- Spain.


In heading straight for Trini-

doned the idea of travelling the
comparatively safer but longer
routes eastward and westward.


The only inhabitants Of the
jungles over which the Lind
berghs are flying are three semi
civilized Indian tribes. the Cara
hyounas, the Carahyabas, and the
Nayamaras. Their only connec-
ton with the outside world Is

Trinidad route were suit
able for an emergency landing Of

landing over the greater part OF

crash.

northeasterly direction over the
Negro river, and then headed due
north when they came to the

SKOPLJE, Yugoslavia @.-The
Dancing Dervishes are not downhearted.
- Suppressed in modern Turkey. and
elsewhere referred to as a dying sect,
they carry on their strange worship
here as though nothing had happened.
the threshold of extinction, the Der
x.snes OF Skoplje are preparing placldly
and methodically for long future.


The sheik of the Skoplje Dervishes Is
well along in years: SO his son Is his
understudy, his grandson also practices
the ritual and his 4-year-old great
grandson is already in active training
for period of leadership hardly likely
to begin before 1878.


An observer finally managed to ma
neuver his way into a Dervish dance,
but not by asking guides. who professed
complete ignorance of what was going
on among the Dervishes.


In Darkened House.


1t was one of King Alexander's gen.
darmes who revealed the place Of the
dance.


The narrow. cobbled street was dark.
The Dervish tekke injecting house, it
sell WdS llUJ JUO VI lilldllJly ASllICo. 1uo
it was plain that what was going on In
the center of the little hall was a re-
ligious ceremony. Under the yellow light
of some old electric bulbs and a kero-
sene lamp about 40 men and boys knelt
on goatSkin rugs and bent their fore
heads to the floor IN prayer.


Before them, where the altar might
have been in church, was niche in
which hung knives and swords. and
Scourages with sharp pointed handles OF
steel. Youngest of the worshipers was
the old sheik's great-grandson, black
robed and obedient, but with the merry
look of a 4-year-old having q grand
time


The child followed the ritual closely,
watching the other Dervishes out Of the
corner of one eye, bowling when they
bowed kneeling when they knelt and
babbling after them the words of the
monotonous chants. Behind wooden
balustrades on two sides of the hall sat
or stood the spectators, including the
women.


Faster and Faster.


Gradually more muscles were brought
into play by the worshipers. Whereas
at first they had only knelt on their
rugs and meditated or chanted, bowling
their heads to the floor. they now
formed sWaying lines, circling sideways
around the hall with arms interlocked,
lunging forward and bending backward
in unison, uttering monotonous chant
which gradually became louder and
faster.


Now whirling dervishes. reverently
rotating their weird. wide skirts like
inverted lilies, came between the sway
ing lines of men and boys and whirled
around, around, around. -.


The swaying lines of bowling, lunging.
lurching men moved faster. The chant
of many voices became one compelling
voice and the tireless lunging and bend
ing of the bodies seemed the writhing
and bending of a composite creature.


Then suddenly there were individuals
again, men from the lines who came
forward toward the niche, where now
the venerable bearded sheik stood and
distributed the Scourges. Each man as
he received the scourge bowed his head
before the sheik, who smiled benevo-
lently and touched his lips to the wor-
shippers hair.


Frenz;ed Chanting.


The men still in the lines, or seated,
chanting. on the floor, shouted rhythmi-
cally their encouragement as the bearers
of the scourges danced slowly around
the hall, twirling the sharp-pointed
steel handles gainst their collar bones.
The chanting became frenzied. The
steel points glittered: the chains and
studded thongs of the scourges struck
the backs of the worshipers.


Again the pace quickened; the points
flashed One after another of the
dervishes thrust the sharp steel through
his cheeks. With the steel in his flesh
he danced on; then withdrew it and
reverently returned the scourge to the
sheik.


The little 4-year-old Dervish in the
black robe toddled across the floor to
his great-grandfather and reached en-
Enthusiastically toward a scourge. The
old man smilingly waved him away.


The ceremony was over.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico, March A.
Twenty persons are known to have lost
their lives when the River Yaguez,
flooded by heavy rains, rose 7 feet and
poured into the town of Mayaguez last
night, causing great property damage.


The water supply was ruined, electric
light service was halted, and most of
the telephone lines were broken. Com
munication with Mayaguez was difficult,
but the district attorney got through by
telephone this evening to report that 20
bodies had been recovered and that the
search for others was continuing.


The Yaguez empties into the ocean
at Mayaguez, and at the mouth is the
city's shipping and wholesale business
district. Hundreds of homes along the
river bank were carried out to sea during
the night.


Some fear was felt for q mission
maintained by the Presbyterian Mission
Board in conjunction with which a
church, school and a dispensary are
operated.

England.

the Queen Anne dover house.

thatched roofs. Now they loath
the gables and dislike the thatched
roof because of the bugs and in
SectS they encourage.


Modern architecture is the rage,
with the straight roof line, and
windows designed to allow the
suns rays to penetrate, and with
a roof that will throw off the
rain.


But instead Of pulling down the
old manor house they are rebuild
ing it, and leaving the old designs
to the jerry builder to hide.

finest Scotch whiskies selling at a
dollar quart in bond, Americans with
bright ideas about sending Christmas

lens involved in taking advantage of

text:
HE depression breathed new
life into the ghost towns and


near ghost towns of the old


gold-mining West. Where desc


late, empty wooden buildings
for a generation or more clustered for
lornly about the gaping mouths of un-
used mine shafts, the last few years
have brought again the busy clatter of
the hammer, the thrilling roar of the
stamp mill, the sight of contented faces
and the Tilt of happy voices. Spectral
townships once more are flushed with
life


But fortune turns and swings in the
slightest breeze. Again the existence of
these rejuvenated communities is
threatened. The events of the last month
or two, coming as bolt from the blue,
seem likely to turn these bustling COM
munities back into the ghost towns that
they were for so long.


: And, oddly enough, the same wheel
of fortune which threatens now to bring
the second death of these old ghostly
centers of our days of golden prosperity
may, at the same time, bring the spark
of life back into the ghost towns of silver
fame They were not reborn along with
the forgotten cities of the gold-produc-
ing areas-they slumbered on in dreary
inactivity. Now they, too, may know
second life, may be turned again into
bustling, prosperous communities.
-OUT in California the gold-mining
towns of Grass Valley, Placerville,
Nevada City, Jackson, Eldorado and
Downieville, nesting in the High Sierras,
do not have the riotous life and wealth
that they knew during the latter half
Of the nineteenth century, when gold
was still the States principal source of
wealth. But since 1929 they have come
long way back toward their former
glory. These towns, along with others
in Nevada, Placer, Amador and Eldorado
Counties, in California, and in the gold
mining sections of Utah, South Dakota,
Nevada, Colorado and Arizona, are once
more alive after years of browsing in
semi-oblivion.


The old stagecoach does not swing
along the dusty California trails, carry
ing miners, gamblers, fancy ladies and
gold to Sacramento and San Francisco
from the distant East and the nearer
mountains, but new automobiles now
swiftly skim the smooth highways where
until recently there was only silence and
tall trees. The rough amuSementS of
earlier days-gambling, great drinking
bouts, dance-hall carousing and frequent
set-tos with knives and pistols-may be
a part of the exciting past, but new
motion picture theaterS, lighted store
fronts and bustling throngs of workers
and their families now take the place
Of inactivity and despair.


But this new vitality must soon make
way for the old desolation unless there
comes some change in the Presidents
embargo on gold exports. Bankers and
economists may theorize over the effects
of Americas REIMBURSEMENT of the gold
standard the general public may debate
the pros and cons of gold and its con-
nection with world events, but to the
miner the problem is simple and direct
It means that the ghost towns, granted
brief respite from limbo, must return
to antiquity. 1t means the sleeping again
under the Summer sun and the Winter
snow of towns that are now thriving
and prosperous.


But let us, for a moment, look back so
years or so. There was then gold
for the mining in CALIFORNIA; mountains.

HAVANA, Aug. 7 0N.S0-A
reported military uprising against
the regime of President Gerardo
Machado was apparently quelled
within a few hours today.


Reports from reliable sources
stated 400 soldiers attached to
Camp Colombia revolted, but
speedy action by loyal troops put
down the rebellion.


Several Skirmishes Fought


Several Skirmishes we're re-
ported to have occurred before
the attempted coup d'etat was
frustrated. For more than an
hour, the sound of canonading
came from the Cabanas fortress,
but at II a. m. the firing died
down. FusilladeS continued to
be heard, however, at intervals.


The reported uprising climaXed
q widespread "strike rebellion"
against the Machado regime,
which paralyzed the nations in
dustry.


The menacing situation result
ing from the strike and the fir
ing from the Cabanas fortress
denuded the streets Of pedeS-
trians.


The famous Prado, favorite
gathering place of American tour
lists, was virtually empty save for
heavily armed policemen. The
National Hotel and other estab-
1ishments frequented by Ameri-
cans were heavily guarded.


Strike Grips All Cities


Passengers arriving from Amer
lean ships landed without diff
Guilty, but an atmosphere Of ten
sion pervaded the city. Reports
from the interior indicated the
strike had gripped all cities in an
iron grasp.


Despite apparent suppression OF
the revolt, the situation in Hav'
ana and elsewhere throughout the
republic remained menacing.


Two persons we're shot and
killed by secret service operatives
during a serious riot, bringing the
total killed since the strike started
20 "A, in Havana alone.


Executive personnel Of down
town offices worked behind closed
doors. The city was almost with
out food, baked ham from storage
and water being almost the sole
fare.


Serious Riots RepOrted
Serious riots were reported In
Camaguey, where person was
killed and IL wounded.


Meanwhile a checkup revealed
the rebellion against the Machado
regime has taken a toll OF II
dead and $50 wounded.


While Machado has thus far
abstained from declaring martial
law for fear widespread disorders
and bloodshed will result, he has
proclaimed Cuba "a state of in
tense agitation" and authorized
the army to preserve order in
whatever manner necessary"


While Congress is expected to
grant Machado's demands, there
were reports the nationwide strike
might embolden the legislators to
ask the President to resign as the
easiest means of restoring normal
conditions.


The Cuban senate today passed
a bill authorizing President
Machado to proclaim martial law.
The bill now goes to the lower
house.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind, November A.
In the greatest concentration Of force
since the World War Indiana armed this
week to put an end to the bandit
forays which have terrorized the State
for weeks.


Six hundred picked ridemen from the
National Guard were ordered out by
Gov. Paul v. McNutt to supplement the
State police force, while virtually all
Of the 302 American Legion posts or
ganized volunteer shotgun" squads TO
cooperate with local law enforcement
agencies.


The National Guardsmen were divided
into two sections. One group was formed
into flying squadrons equipped with
fast automobiles and armed with
purposes The other and larger group
was divided among various districts
with orders to blockade roads at night,
where all who pass are to be questioned
and searched.


Orders Of shoot to kill" accompanied
the mobilization of the Guardsmen
While the soldiers are blockading the
roads plain clOtheSmen from the State

Government operatives are conducting
a quiet hunt which has for its purpose
the capture of the eight convicts who
shot their way out Of the Indiana State
Prison at Michigan City month ago

the bandttry.

Armstrong, called upon 10000 Legion
aires to respond. Local posts have or
ganized squads armed with shotguns

local police officials and sheriffs.
